en: Now begins the eighth chapter:
But the king, desiring to examine legal cases, should enter the court modestly, together with Brahmins, as well as with ministers skilled in counsel. 8.1.

The protection of subjects is ordained as the livelihood of a king, and that is established here: "Bearing weapons and missiles is the means of subsistence for the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture for the Vaiśya; and service to the twice-born for the Śūdra" (MDh 10.79).
"A king who conducts himself in this manner attains the unsurpassed worlds.

Thus, righteousness increases in the world. Furthermore, there is indeed the right to sovereignty for members of other castes as well who live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya. For it is traditionally taught: "Whoever is the protector of all people is known as a king."
And devotion to action is prescribed for the common welfare of the world.

Protection consists in the removal of suffering. Suffering is twofold: visible and invisible. Among these, the visible suffering is the oppression of the weak by the strong through the seizure of wealth and other such means. For the other, however, invisible suffering is the production of misery in the next world through the demerit (*pratyavāya*) born of transgressing the injunctions. For subjects, acting improperly toward one another due to hatred, envy, and so forth, follow wrong paths and would be oppressed by the fault of their unseen karma (*adṛṣṭa-doṣa*). Consequently, the kingdom would perish; for sovereignty over the subjects is called "kingdom. When they are perishing, whose kingdom would it be? Therefore, legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*) and the rest must be settled by the punishment prescribed in the scriptures; thus, being restrained by fear, they do not deviate separately from the path, and in both ways they are protected. Furthermore, the king’s fines consist of taxes, duties, and the like. Since there is no other righteous livelihood besides this, the ruin of the kingdom would result from the loss of its means of subsistence (*vṛtti-parikṣaya*). Therefore, for the sake of maintaining the kingdom, the administration of justice (*vyavahāra-darśana*) must be performed.

This is now stated: here, "legal procedure" (*vyavahāra*) refers to the activity of the plaintiff and defendant for the purpose of mutually refuting and establishing their respective positions. Alternatively, it means that the very subjects of dispute—such as the non-payment of debts and so forth—being the objects of contention, must be made fit for the scope of investigation. By stating "desiring to see," there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the phrase "he shall look into the cases" (MDh 8.2). Furthermore, there is a subsequent reference: "of these, the first is the non-payment of debts" (MDh 8.4). The connection is: "he should investigate those subjects. A "court" (*sabhā*) is a place presided over by the person authorized to speak as will be described later. "Entry" (*praveśa*) is the act of entering into its interior. Does he enter alone? No; the author says, "together with Brāhmaṇas. Now, to whom does the qualification "versed in counsel" (*mantrajña*) apply? It cannot apply to the ministers, because their status as ministers is already established by that very title; indeed, one who does not know counsel cannot be called a minister. Nor can it apply to the Brāhmaṇas, because if they were merely authorized to observe the legal proceedings, their knowledge of such counsel would serve no unseen spiritual purpose (*adṛṣṭa*).

To this it is replied: This is indeed a qualification of the Brahmins. For they, being ignorant of counsel (*amantrajña*), might act with reckless determination; otherwise, they would bring misfortune upon the king. To illustrate: if someone relying on a high minister transacts business with a common subject and is suddenly defeated, yet is neither punished nor made to pay the fine by seizing his wealth, then the administration of justice would not have been conducted with impartiality. The subjects would then perceive either partiality or incapacity on the part of the king. If, on the other hand, he is punished, there may be a disturbance of the state due to the agitation of the high minister. But those who are experts in counsel, being cautious, might—under some pretext regarding the matter to be decided—halt the proceedings and privately inform the king: "Between these two litigants, this one is defeated and that one wins; however, we have not yet reached a final decision on the case, so Your Majesty is the ultimate authority. Thereupon, the king, having understood this, instructs the high minister: "Your man has been defeated; let there be no ruin for me, so the decision has been temporarily set aside. You yourself must act in such a way that this man is reconciled and his grievance is removed. These ministers, whose words are authoritative, thus prevent all harmful conduct among the people.

Others, however, consider the term *mantrajña* to be a qualifier for both [the ministers and the Brahmins] according to their respective meanings, like the eye of a crow. When the ministers are the subject qualified, *mantrajñatva* consists in the knowledge of those various elements (*dhātu*) and their application. In the case of the Brahmins, however, it refers to the balanced deliberation on the matter at hand. It is not merely that the ministers and Brahmins enter [the court]; rather, they must "observe the decision" (*paśyet*), as indicated by the subsequent sentence (MDh 8.2). This is appropriate because otherwise, their entry would be for the sake of some invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, one should not make a decision alone, but rather after deliberating with them.

He should be disciplined, free from fickleness of speech, hands, and feet; for from trembling, indeed, misfortune arises. Because of the mention of the "king" (*pārthiva*), this instruction does not apply to the Kṣatriya alone; rather, it applies to any other lord of the earth, a ruler of a region, for otherwise the kingdom would not remain stable. (8.1)
Seated there or even standing, having raised his right hand and being modest in dress and ornaments, he should examine the legal cases of the litigants.

"Sitting" means seated upon the seat of justice (*dharmāsana*). "Standing" means not sitting down at all, having refrained from walking about. There is an option between standing and sitting depending on the specific nature of the case: in a serious matter requiring much to be said, he should be seated; in a minor matter requiring little to be said, he should remain standing. Walking about is prohibited altogether, for one intent on looking at the road would not be able to attentively grasp the precise statements of the plaintiff and the defendant.
Others, however, consider it to have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*): when ascetics, brahmins, and so forth are standing, he stands; when they are sitting, he sits.

"Raising the hand" means raising the upper arm and standing up; this is a deviation from the rule established by the author of the Sūtras, for it is always prescribed that one should sit with the *upavyāna* (the sacred thread) over the left shoulder. Therefore, the meaning is this: the hand should be lifted, but it should not be kept touching something nearby. Furthermore, at the time of answering a question or when a prohibition is issued, he should signal by that [gesture], and not by moving forward or other such actions. By this observation of his conduct, the underlying intention (*tātparya*) is made known. For generally, men raise their hands when they are exerting effort in their tasks. If the king were to walk while sitting comfortably, then the attendants would think: "The king does not pay attention to us, and we have been defeated by the members of the court (*sabhyas*) who are acting without fear. The mention of the "hand" (*pāṇi*) is intended to indicate the entire arm (*bāhu*), for the mere movement of the hand alone during the course of legal proceedings would cause distress. Moreover, this instruction is not for the sake of some invisible spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

"Clad in modest dress and ornaments": In the preceding verse, the purpose of restraining the objects of the external and internal senses was stated. This [present verse], however, is for the sake of allowing people to approach him with ease due to his modesty. For if he were dressed in ostentatious attire, there would be a failure of understanding among such people. Therefore, he should never have ostentatious dress or ornaments. "Dress" (*veṣa*) refers to specific arrangements of hair, clothing, and so forth; "ornaments" (*ābharaṇa*) refers to earrings and the like. In that context, "ostentatious dress" means wearing garments with hems turned up, or wearing swift-moving red robes, and so on. "Ostentatious ornaments" means being adorned with many brilliant jewels and many necklaces. For he would be as difficult for ordinary people—and especially for those engaged in legal matters—to look upon as the sun itself. "He should see" states the purpose of entering the assembly. "The discerning man should see."

And this instruction for the king regarding the administration of justice shall extend up to the determination of the matter according to its proper place. Its essential purpose is that the authority for protection should be exercised by him alone; since such an audience [of justice] is impossible for others, they have no such authority. However, the examination of legal cases—which has as its sole fruit the severing of doubts for all—is indeed available to a learned Brāhmaṇa, just like the instruction on penance (*prāyaścitta*). For it is said: "One should speak in matters of legal difficulty. Likewise, there is an appointment to examine such legal cases for those belonging to a single group—such as merchants, farmers, herdsmen, and so forth—in the event of a dispute over the customary rules of their own group or in other matters, because prosperity results from a superior decision. For it has been stated: * *ayaṃ ca rājño darśanāpadeśo daṇḍapraṇayane yathāsthānārthapratipādanaparyanto bhaviṣyati | tātparyaṃ tasyaiva rakṣādhikāraḥ prayuktaḥ syāt | īdṛśasya ca darśanasyānyeṣām asaṃbhāvanād anadhikāraḥ | sarveṣāṃ saṃśayacchedamātraphalaṃ tu vyavahāradarśanaṃ prāyaścittopadeśavad viduṣo brāhmaṇasyāsty eva | uktaṃ hi "dharmasaṃkaṭeṣu brūyāt" iti | tathaikavargyāṇāṃ vāṇijyakarṣakapaśupālaprabhṛtīnāṃ svavargasāmayikārthavipratipattāv anyasyāṃ votkṛṣṭanirṇayād bhūtir iti tathāvidhavyavahāradarśane niyogaḥ | tathā hi paṭhitam |* And this instruction for the king regarding the administration of justice shall extend up to the determination of the matter according to its proper place. Its essential purpose is that the authority for protection should be exercised by him alone; since such an audience [of justice] is impossible for others, they have no such authority. However, the examination of legal cases—which has as its sole fruit the severing of doubts for all—is indeed available to a learned Brāhmaṇa, just like the instruction on penance (*prāyaścitta*). For it is said: "One should speak in matters of legal difficulty. Likewise, there is an appointment to examine such legal cases for those belonging to a single group—such as merchants, farmers, herdsmen, and so forth—in the event of a dispute over the customary rules of their own group or in other matters, because prosperity results from a superior decision. For it has been stated:
"Families, guilds, assemblies, and the appointed king are the foundations of legal proceedings; each subsequent one is more authoritative than the preceding.

(NSm Mā 1.7) In this context, "families" refers to a group of kinsmen. One must not deviate from the decision made by them. If they do not place their trust in that, saying, "These [others] are our closer relatives," then it should be reported to the guilds (*śreṇi*).

"Guilds" (*śreṇayaḥ*) refers to merchants and others who live by a common trade. Among these, guilds possess greater authority than kinsmen. For kinsmen do not restrain one who has strayed from the duties of their lineage out of fear of violating family law; however, guilds deliberate after taking sureties for the purpose of preventing deviation, thinking: "If one deviates from this, punishment must be imposed in the assembly, or you must not be allowed to stray," because the guild's integrity perishes through approaching the king and being subjected to the entry of royal officials, which leads to its humiliation.

"Ganas" refers to those who move about in groups, such as temple priests (*maṭhabrāhmaṇa*) and others who construct houses, palaces, and so forth. They shall oversee the legal proceedings of their own members. In that regard, *upasadas* (supervisors) must be appointed for the sake of ensuring stability. The distinction is this: whereas previously those who lived by the same profession acted alone, these [members of the *gaṇas*] act collectively. Because they act collectively, litigants from the *śreṇis* (guilds) are [preferred], as they possess knowledge of the facts due to their collective nature. Others, however, say that "families" (*kulāni*) refers to impartial men; for they, being insiders to the matter and not belonging to any guild, are the ones who decide.

The "authorized" [person] is the learned Brāhmaṇa versed in the three Vedas (*traividya*), for it is ordained that he shall act as the proclaimer in matters of legal difficulty (*dharmasaṃkaṭa*). His superiority over the former [the king] is due to his learning (*vaiduṣya*); the king’s superiority, however, is due to his exceptional power (*atiśayaśakti*). Therefore, when a decision has been made by the king himself, who is learned, this [objection] does not apply.
"One who thinks 'I am not defeated' even though he has been defeated according to justice—having imposed a double fine, the king should reopen that case. (NSm Mā 1.56) (YDh 2.309)

This applies to other legal proceedings; for in those cases, there is an occasion for further speech, as one might ask, "What will he say now that the matter has been correctly adjudicated by the authorized officials but remains to be decided by the king?"

Another interpretation: by kings, a "superintendent" is a Brahmin acting in the capacity of a royal official. Likewise, for another householder, there certainly exists a judicial proceeding extending even to punishment, based on the traditional rule that "the master of the house is independent within his own home"; this is for the sake of training the latent tendencies and ensuring that disciples, sons, and others who are subject to the authority of the scriptures are properly examined. For a minor offense, the householder himself acts like a king; however, in the case of a major transgression, it is appropriate to report it to the king—this is the meaning.

Therefore, the objection raised by some—having superimposed the status of an *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) upon the phrase "he should see," and thereby suspected that only Brāhmaṇas and others have the qualification (*adhikāra*), and subsequently supported that view with great effort—is incorrect. This is because the subject matter differs and the qualifications differ. For the king’s own domain extends up to the infliction of punishment, whereas for Brāhmaṇas and others, it extends only up to the judicial decision (*nirṇaya*). The qualification (*adhikāra*) is likewise distinct: for the king, the purpose is the stability of the kingdom; for the others, it consists in benefiting others through the resolution of doubts and so forth. Consequently, there is no possibility whatsoever of a confusion of functions (*vṛtti-saṃkara*). Rather, the removal of conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti-nirāsa*) is the task at hand. For when litigants are in conflict, the king must establish equality during the investigation of the legal case (*vyavahāra-darśana*). If he does not, then what restraint would there be on the king’s own acquisition of wealth when they reach an agreement? For we shall explain later [in verse 8.2] that one who is pure in body has no restriction regarding dogs. 8.2 ||
Day by day, through reasons observed in the world and observed in the scriptures, [these matters] were recorded separately according to eighteen different categories. (8.3)

By the first half [of the verse], the grounds for decision (*nirṇayahetu*) are stated; by the second half, the enumeration of the titles of law (*vivādapada*) is indicated. The words "he shall examine" (*paśyet*) and "the cases" (*kāryāṇi*) are supplied from the preceding verse. He shall examine the cases every day; that is, as each day passes, the adjudication of legal disputes (*vyavahāranirṇaya*) must be carried out. Regarding the phrase "by means of grounds" (*hetubhiḥ*): a ground (*hetu*) is the instrument of decision. It is of two kinds: that which takes the form of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that which takes the form of a formal settlement (*vyavasthā*). Among these, the ground for deciding the matter that takes the form of a means of valid cognition consists of witnesses and so forth. The ground that takes the form of a formal settlement is that by which a legal proceeding is concluded even when there is no certain determination of the matter through [ordinary] means of knowledge. For example, an oath of truth, or a single witness agreed upon by both parties—if his status as a means of valid cognition is accepted by the plaintiff and the defendant—he becomes a ground for decision even if he has not been examined by the members of the court (*sabhyas*). However, there can be no determination of the matter based on the word of an unexamined person if his reliability (*āptatva*) is not known. Even when the judges (*prāśnikas*) accept it, it serves as a ground for the formal settlement.

That legal arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is of two kinds: common (*sādhāraṇī*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇī*). It is also twofold based on the difference of region and the difference of substratum: non-contradictory (*aviruddhā*) and contradictory (*viruddhā*). The non-contradictory is, for example, that among certain Southerners (*dākṣiṇātyānām*), when a sonless woman ascends the funeral pillar (*sabhāsthāṇu*) upon the death of her husband, once she has ascended it and been examined by the authorities, she is marked with the appropriate signs and immediately thereafter receives the inheritance from among the sapinda relatives. Likewise, among the Northerners (*udīcām*), if food is given to one who asks for a girl being sought in marriage, then even if it is not explicitly said, "She is given to you," she becomes betrothed. The contradictory is, for instance, that in some regions grain is lent in the spring and received back doubled in the autumn. Similarly, a pledge (*ādhi*) whose enjoyment has been authorized continues to be used even after the interest on the loan has reached double, until the principal gold has been paid back. For this [practice] is contradictory to such rules as: "He may take an eightieth part [as interest]" (MDh 8.140) and "Interest on a loan shall not exceed double [the principal]" (MDh 8.151).

In this context, those [grounds for proof] based on distinctions are designated by the term "reasons seen in local custom" (*deśadṛṣṭahetu*). However, reasons seen in the scriptures (*śāstradṛṣṭahetu*) are those recited in the treatises. Among these, some are rules devised by the authors of the treatises, while others are restated exactly as they exist in reality. Regarding that, an example of a rule devised by the authors is: documentary evidence (*lekhya*), possession (*upabhoga*), and witnesses (*sākṣin*). On the other hand, inference (*anumāna*) is fixed upon the actual state of things, as in: "Just as a hunter follows the track of a deer by the drops of blood" (MDh 8.44). Although not everything worldly obtains its authority from the words of the authors of the treatises, nevertheless, even that which is purely worldly must in certain cases rely upon the treatise. For instance, when it is stated that "in such an offense this ordeal [is applicable]" or "possession for such a length of time is authoritative," even though that is worldly, it is said to be "seen in the scriptures. Within that established rule, if the basis of the authors of the treatises is possible, it is authoritative; however, that whose basis is impossible is not to be respected. An example is the recitation of the procedure for drawing up documents: [The text continues with the technical details of document preparation.]
"Thus, at the request of both parties, this has been written by me, the son of so-and-so; let the scribe named so-and-so write it according to the truth. (YDh 2.91)

If the scribe should record his own name at the very beginning, stating, “I, named so-and-so, the son of such-and-such, write this,” there would be no fault. He records his name for this purpose: so that the scribe may be identified by the statement, “This was written by him. For if that scribe is already established as trustworthy through other means of proof (*pramāṇa*), then what he has written is authoritative. And if he were not to identify himself by his own family name (*gotra-nāman*), then whose trustworthiness would one seek to verify through other means? However, if recognition should occur—either through the sight of another document or by some other reason—that he is a distinguished scribe, then even if he is not explicitly identified, there is no fault. In that case, even if the scribe does not write, “This was written by me,” such a document would indeed possess all its required characteristics. And this examination of the scribe is useful in that context. Here, the scribe is included among the witnesses because other witnesses are few in number. But where there are many other trustworthy witnesses who have set their own hands [to the document], there the trustworthiness pertaining to the scribe is of no use. Such is another settled rule.
A document is [validated] by another document, and testimony by witnesses;
yet a document is superior to witnesses, and witnesses are [superior] to a document. (NSm 1.125)

Even in this arrangement, there is no basis whatsoever [for such a distinction]. For documentary evidence (*lekhyam*) is of two kinds: that executed by one's own hand and that executed by another's hand. That executed by another's hand is also of two kinds: that written by a scribe using his own hand and that written by an authorized scribe. This entire category of evidence executed by another's hand consists solely of witnesses, because in that case the distinction [implied by the phrase] "documentary evidence from witnesses" (*sākṣibhyo likhitam*) would be untenable. Indeed, its definition is as follows: "The witnesses, with their own hands, preceded by the names of their fathers and so forth..."
"In that case, [the witnesses] should write together: 'I, so-and-so, am a witness. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.89) Thus it is said.

Nor is the validity of a document written by a single hand accepted, just as [the testimony of] a single witness is not. If it is argued that this distinction is the reason for its superiority—namely, that witnesses have committed their signatures to the document itself—it does not become superior on account of this specific feature. For trustworthiness is the cause of superiority, and that must be examined in both cases alike. Therefore, regarding such a document, the rule concerning conflicting witnesses applies: "One should accept the majority" (MDh 8.73). Furthermore, being appointed by the king is not a distinguishing factor; the advantage there lies in the fact that one who has been examined is then appointed. And not all those appointed by the king are necessarily well-examined. However, if such a person were free from defects and possessed of extreme excellence, he alone might indeed serve as a corroborator. For instance, royal land-grant charters (*agrahāra-śāsana*) written by a single scribe’s hand do indeed become authoritative. The "signature of the giver" (*svāhastakya*) is his own admission: "This much was received by me from him," and "this must be given to him. In that case, if he later says, "It was not received," then he is defeated by those who cite what was previously recorded. In such a situation, there is no occasion for witnesses at all.

But surely, if it is understood from a certain document that "this was admitted by him," yet at a later time he himself says, "it was not received," then between these two admissions, for what reason should the latter be sublated by the former, and not the former by the latter? Since they are equal in status, there is doubt due to contradiction; therefore, it is proper to employ another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

This would indeed be so if there were equality [of status]. For the admission that "it was not received" can occur even through greed and other such motives; however, no sane person, having not actually received it, would say "it was received. Even in that case, if he should say "it was returned," yet no written document was produced because of absence, and a counter-document was not obtained because the scribe was absent due to being preoccupied with another urgent matter—then in this situation, there is simply no occasion for other means of proof, such as witnesses and the like.

As for the rule that "a document is [cancelled] by another document," this technical convention cannot override an understanding derived from the inherent nature of the facts. Indeed, we see creditors gradually clearing a debt while holding the document in their hands, yet they do not record on the back of the document that the money has been cleared, saying: "Today this much has been paid; tomorrow I will bring more and, having combined it, I shall credit the total; or else, after clearing the whole amount within a few days, I will tear up the document. This is because the matter concerns a different substance (the debt itself). Furthermore, when a creditor is pressed by a debtor who is unable to pay the principal, interest, and fees, and the debtor offers only the portion that clears the balance, how can the creditor enforce the rule: "He shall not pay until a counter-document has been given"? If this convention were strictly "only by another document," then how could a case involving fraud or duress (*balopadhikṛtatva*) be investigated? For in such cases, the possibility of another document does not exist. Therefore, just as in this case where, even though a document exists, other means of proof (*pramāṇāntara*) are employed to ascertain its validity, so too should they be employed elsewhere. For example, someone might state: "I went to his confidence and executed a document; he said, 'Take this sum of money now for the auspicious occasion (*puṇyāha*), and tomorrow I will give you the rest,' and having said this, he gave only that sum and did not give the remainder. In such a case, there is certainly an occasion to employ other means of proof. In that situation, if the debtor has witnesses regarding this matter, then once the document has been challenged and shown to be spurious, the creditor must prove the payment made the following day. If, however, this convention between the two was made in secret, then there is an occasion for divine ordeals (*daivī kriyā*). But if even there one lacks confidence due to the possibility of error, the settlement must be made by a truthful oath (*satyaśapatha*).

But if this is so, then a document written by one's own hand (*svahastalekhya*) would indeed be invalid, because it depends on the corroboration of other means of proof. In that case, there would be a contradiction with the [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra] rules: "It is established even without witnesses" (YDh 2.92) and "marked with one's own hand" (YDh 2.96). By this same logic, one might not see a substance being given directly before one's eyes; rather, having received it in their presence, one merely declares: "This much has been taken by me from him. Those [people present] could also be witnesses. In that instance too, it could be said: "Having gained confidence in him, I accepted [the debt]."

It has been stated here that the actual state of things cannot be subverted by a contradiction with scripture (*smṛti*). Furthermore, this statement will serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only where it finds its proper application; it does not apply everywhere. For instance, consider a document held in the hand of a creditor for a long time: if the debt has indeed been paid by him, how could it be that he neither requested the document nor had it surrendered? Indeed, such long-term neglect of a matter like this is impossible. Rather, his status as a liar is inferred from this. And so it has been said:
"In matters requiring action, one should report the king's strength [of the case] either immediately or after three days.

In a case where there is a pledge for use (*bhogyabandha*) but no specific period of enjoyment has been stipulated, if a dispute arises, even in the absence of witnesses, a document in one's own hand (*svahastalekhya*) is decisive; for debtors cannot say, "This was said by you out of friendship, now abandon it," nor is there an occasion for the previously mentioned statement: "I will give it after the document is prepared," followed by "It was not given. If it was not given, how could the enjoyment of the pledge have been tolerated?

But if this is so, then possession accompanied by a written document would be the means of proof; yet they declare that mere possession is authoritative, as in: "A document, witnesses, and possession" (NSm 1.65). Why do we question what has already been answered? It is not mere possession that is the means of proof, but possession qualified by time. For it is recited thus: "Whatever [has been enjoyed] for ten years... (MDh 8.147), and likewise: "The loss of land occurs after twenty years for one who sees and does not speak" (YDh 2.24).
What, then, is the meaning of the statement: "A written document [is invalidated] by a written document alone" (NSm 1.125)?

This has been explained by others: when there is doubt regarding the specific author—namely, whether this was written by such-and-such a person or not—it is ascertained by means of a document whose author is certain. As for that which was executed in the presence of witnesses, the witnesses remove any doubt as to whether it was done or not; they alone are the authority in that case. In such instances, the production of another document made by that same person is not required. Furthermore, in cases involving intentional acts such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth, a document is superior to mere witnesses. For witnesses might forget, or enter into a relationship with one of the parties, or encounter some other reason for disqualification as witnesses due to sin. A document, however, being under the control of the plaintiff, is well-protected and thus superior to witnesses. This very point is stated: "But [witnesses are set aside] by a document" (NSm 1.125). By means of a document established by one's own hand, even a forgotten matter is considered to have occurred. Or, if the witnesses have died, they become authoritative through the recognition of their handwriting.

Other commentaries have been correctly composed by Bhartṛyajña himself; they should be understood from that very source as being entirely rooted in authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). One must follow the established rules regarding the causes of legal memory (*smṛti*). Nor is it proper to assume that legal memory alone constitutes an authoritative means of knowledge. For it cannot be said that the memory of legal procedure (*vyavahāra-smṛti*) is based on the Veda, because the modes of victory and defeat are matters of established fact (*siddhārtha*), being cognizable through perception and other means. Indeed, this matter is already established: "In such a legal proceeding, one party loses and the other wins. As for the indicative Vedic text (*liṅga-śruti*) cited here, it is to be understood as being like the injunction, "One desiring health should eat *harītakī*. Since the purpose regarding the purification of substances has already been examined in connection with such injunctions, we shall not labor over it again.

Among the eighteen paths, the path (*mārga*) is the subject of dispute; it is with reference to these matters that people generally engage in debate. "Established tasks" (*nibaddhāni kāryāṇi*) refers to purposes, that is to say, the accomplishment of aims. We shall demonstrate those later on. He states their individual preeminence: these are distinct purposes and do not, moreover, subsume one another, as other [categories] are subsumed under the "incidental" (*anuṣaṅga*) and so forth. These are not like that; however, there are thousands of incidental [purposes]. (8.3)
Of these, the first is non-payment of debt, followed by deposits, sale without ownership, partnership, and the non-delivery of what has been given. (8.4)
The non-payment of wages, the breach of an agreement, rescission of purchase and sale, and disputes between an owner and a herdsman; 8.5.
The law concerning boundary disputes; verbal and physical assault;
theft; violence; and the abduction of women. (8.6)
The duties of women and men, partition [of inheritance], gambling, and betting—these eighteen are the topics in this world for the administration of legal procedure. (8.7)

The status of *ṛṇādāna* as the first [topic] is either in reference to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)—meaning its primacy—or it is primary (*mukhya*). For by this [latter sense], even those living in the forest are touched upon. Furthermore, there is the non-payment of debt (*anṛṇādāna*) which is connected to the payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*), such as: "I have paid your debt; give me a document of clearance," and so forth. This is not [strictly] *ṛṇādāna*, but because it is mentioned therein, it is designated as such. Likewise:
"The debt that is to be paid and that which is not to be paid, by whom, where, and how, as well as the rules for giving and receiving"—(NSm 1.1).

In that regard, the debt to be paid is that which was contracted by oneself and that contracted by one's father, as well as by whoever inherits the estate. That which is not to be paid is a debt contracted by oneself exceeding double [the principal], and a debt contracted by a father incurred through gambling and the like—this applies to the son, the husband, and the father respectively. Likewise: "A woman shall not pay a debt contracted by her husband, nor one contracted by her son, except for what she has promised herself, or what may have been contracted jointly with her husband. (NSm 1.13)

Although this is included within the phrase "that which is to be paid," nevertheless, that which is incurred through gambling and the like is payable by its very nature regardless of specific circumstances; however, this [present case] arises from a restriction on the agent (*kartṛniyamāt*), and thus there is a distinction between them like that between "cattle" and "bulls. Furthermore, regarding the limit "up to twice" (*yāvad dvaiguṇyaparyantam*), there is likewise a distinction as previously stated. In the reading "where" (*yatra*), there is the inclusion of place and time: it must be paid in the very same place where it was received; yet, if the creditor so desires, it may be paid in another location. If possible, it may also be paid at another time; for it has been said that one may not demand payment in autumn: "In summer, or when the crops are ripe, or whenever he expects an influx of wealth. Regarding "as much as": if possible, the whole amount; if not, some portion, until it is gradually cleared. "With his entire being" refers to one who is utterly exhausted, as in the rule: "Even by labor, equally" (MDh 8.177). "The rules for giving and receiving" refers to witnesses, written documents, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase *pāruṣye daṇḍavācike*: "staff and speech" is *daṇḍavācam*. By the rule *dvandvāc cudaṣahāntāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.106), the suffix *a* is added at the end of the compound; since this [offense] possesses that [quality], the suffix *ṭhan* is applied by the rule *ata ini ṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.2.115). Regarding the term *strīpuṃdharma*: it is a compound like *śākapārthiva* (king of vegetables), meaning "a man together with a woman. If the analysis were "woman and man," the form would have been *strīpuṃsadharmā*. || 8.4–6 ||
In these matters, regarding men who mostly engage in disputes,
one should carry out the decision of the case by resorting to the eternal dharma.

The inclusion of the word "mostly" (*bhūyiṣṭha*) is for the purpose of indicating preeminence; there are other grounds for legal transactions as well. For example: "You gave me this house for the purpose of dwelling; why then, before a year has passed, do you give it to another? This is not a case of "rescission of what has been given," for in this instance there is no cessation of ownership, but merely permission for the resident to enjoy it. Likewise: "A window was made by you in the house facing my courtyard. Regarding the phrase "relying on eternal dharma": wealth and pleasure are non-eternal. Alternatively, "eternal dharma" refers to that established order which has existed from time immemorial; one should uphold that. However, that which is introduced by people of the present day is not to be respected because of its non-eternality. (8.8)
But when the king himself does not personally oversee legal cases, then he should appoint a learned Brāhmaṇa to oversee those cases. (8.9)
One who is proficient in the eighteen branches of knowledge, designated as a judge (*prāḍvivāka*),
skilled in *ānvīkṣikī*, and devoted to the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.

If, due to preoccupation with some other urgent matter or through lack of proficiency, he should not see [the case] himself, then a learned Brāhmaṇa should be appointed. And that learning which pertains to the subject of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*) is already implied by the very fact of his authority over it; for one who does not know something is not entitled to authority therein. However, the thorough knowledge of the *Dharmaśāstra* serves the purpose of preventing the determination of a contrary meaning through the defects of passion and hatred. A knower of *dharma*, even when passion and hatred are present, does not err out of fear of the scripture; thus, the thorough knowledge of the *Dharmaśāstra* is useful. On the other hand, the observation of legal procedure is implied by its object: the knowledge of that without which the decision of a legal case cannot be made is necessitated by his authority over it. As for that which, having been known, is acted upon otherwise—that cessation [of error] is the subject of another instruction. And he will state this further meaning with another effort: "Three who know the Veda and a learned man appointed by the king" (MDh 8.11). Knowledge of other scriptures, however, would be for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) for one being authorized in legal procedure. It should be read as "a learned man should be appointed" (*niyojyaḥ syāt*); for the Kātyas remember the Ātmanepada suffix in the rule "after a root preceded by a prefix ending in a vowel... (Kātyāyana on Pāṇini 1.3.64). 8.9.
Surrounded by exactly three members of the court, he should examine his legal cases,
having entered the foremost assembly hall, either seated or standing.

By the term "by the members of the assembly" (*sabhyaiḥ*), Brāhmaṇas alone are understood, even though no specific caste is mentioned here, because of the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" later on (MDh 8.11), and because of the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" earlier (MDh 8.1) in the phrase "together with Brāhmaṇas. The mention of "three," however, is for the purpose of excluding one or two; three or more are indeed intended. We shall explain this further in the section on witnesses. Regarding the phrase "having entered the assembly hall itself at its head": since he has already attained the status of the king, his entry into the assembly hall and his presence upon the designated places and seats—which are his duties—would have been implied; the repetition is either for the sake of illustration or to exclude other duties. Therefore, he does not sit in the place of the king. (8.10)
In whatever place three Brahmins learned in the Vedas sit together, along with a learned official of the king, they know that assembly to be a court of Brahmā. (8.11)

It has been stated that, having entered the court (*sabhā*), one should examine legal cases. In common usage, the word *sabhā* refers to a particular type of house or palace, as in the passage: "The divine court, adorned with gold, was constructed by Maya. To exclude the notion that it is merely a gathering of specific individuals, he provides the definition of the court: where three Brahmins learned in the Vedas are present, along with a person related to the king who is appointed and authorized, and is learned—or alternatively, who is "appointed" (*prakṛta*) as mentioned in the immediately preceding verse—that is what is intended here by "court. The mention of "Brahmin" is for the sake of praise; just as the court of Brahmā is irreproachable, so too is this one. (8.11)
When dharma, pierced by adharma, enters an assembly and the members of that assembly do not extract the dart, they themselves are pierced. (8.12)
One should either not enter an assembly or speak what is consistent with the truth;
for a man who remains silent or speaks falsely becomes a sinner. (8.13)

By this meaning, two things are prohibited: one who has accepted the office [of adjudication] must not practice false judgment, nor should he neglect what is being done by another. In both cases there is a fault. If, while another is performing what is contrary [to the law], he remains silent or, by intervention, speaks what is contrary to the scriptures and logic, he becomes a sinner and a partaker of guilt. Therefore, he must not entertain this hope: "The second judge sees falsely and he alone is joined with the sin; as for me, having become silent and indifferent, why should I be joined with the offense? By the prohibition against entering the court, the acceptance of the office of seeing legal proceedings is here forbidden—meaning that the office of seeing legal proceedings should not be undertaken. If, however, one has accepted it, he must speak correctly. But by this [rule], they do not desire silence from a learned man who, though not authorized, happens to be present when the members of the court see falsely. And thus it is said: "Whether appointed or unappointed, one who knows the Dharma ought to speak. If, however, questioning by the king's officers is feared—asking why an unauthorized person speaks—then one should depart from that place. This is what was stated: "And if one is capable, but does not intervene in the injury of the weak" (GDh 21.19). 8.13.
For where dharma is slain by adharma, and truth by falsehood, while those present look on, there the members of the assembly are themselves slain. (8.14)

*Dharma* [94] is a settled order determined by the scriptures, logic, and place. If that is struck down—that is, destroyed—by *adharma* [95], which consists of its transgression, by the plaintiff or the defendant; and likewise, if truth is struck down by falsehood by the witnesses; and if the judges and others merely look on and do not extract the truth, then they too are "struck down," becoming like corpses, and thus they are censured. Therefore, the members of the court must not remain indifferent while the plaintiff and defendant act perversely, nor the witnesses. Although the mention of *dharma* and *adharma* (or the mention of truth and falsehood) would have sufficed for the proof, both are employed here to complete the verse. Thus, it has been explained according to the distinction of their respective objects. 8.14.
Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects.
Therefore, one must not violate Dharma, lest Dharma, being violated, slay us. (8.15)

One must not, out of fear, practice a form of conduct other than the Dharma; for once the Dharma has been transgressed, it destroys—not merely wealth, nor even a king who is its ally. Likewise, the Dharma alone, when protected, dispels all fear. Neither enemies, nor those seeking one's harm, nor even the wrathful can prevail against it. Therefore, knowing this—that "pleasure and pain depend upon the Dharma"—the Dharma must not be violated. If we destroy the Dharma, it strikes back at us like an enraged serpent; thus, lest the Dharma, once destroyed, slay us, it must be guarded for the sake of self-preservation. (8.15)
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed a bull; those who act contrary to him, the gods know as a *vṛṣala*. Therefore, one should not violate the Dharma. (8.16)

By means of the etymological derivation of the word *vṛṣala*, the person of false vision (*mithyādarśin*) is censured. One is not a *vṛṣala* by birth; rather, he is so called because he obstructs (*alamkurute*) *vṛṣa*—that is, Dharma, which rains down [the fulfillment of] desires. The word *alam* signifies cessation. The gods understood this meaning when they said, "He is a *vṛṣala*. As for humans, if they consider it merely a word for a caste, let them do so as they please; however, the gods are more authoritative. And they maintain that the term *vṛṣala* is applied based on this ground for its usage (*pravṛttinimitta*). The mention of the "gods" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Therefore, in such actions as "at the time of a *śrāddha* feast, one must not be approached by *vṛṣalas*" or "a *vṛṣala* who is a thief shall be killed," it is the Brāhmaṇa of false vision alone who is to be understood by the word *vṛṣala*. Thus, thinking "May I not incur the state of being a *vṛṣala*," one should not neglect nor destroy Dharma. The attribution of the state of being a *vṛṣala* is intended as a censure. (8.16)
Dharma alone is the true friend who follows one even unto death;
for all else, including wealth, goes to destruction along with the body. (8.17)

That one must not transgress the Dharma out of fear has been taught by the statement, “Dharma itself, when violated, destroys”; that one must not do so out of affection is what is taught here. Since Dharma alone is the true friend, one should cultivate affection for it. Even another person who is a friend may abandon his life out of regard for some task; even the most intimate friend’s friendship lasts only until death. But Dharma follows a person even after they have died. Therefore, one should not, out of regard for a friend, practice false views or remain indifferent.
Upon the destruction of a man's body, his wife, son, friend, wealth, and inheritance perish;
but dharma alone never abandons him.
Therefore, one should abandon wife and children rather than dharma.

Whatever else there is besides dharma, such as a wife and so forth, all that goes to destruction along with the body. Since no one other than dharma is capable of protecting one who has died, therefore dharma must not be abandoned even out of consideration for friends and kinsmen. (8.17)
One quarter of the sin falls upon the perpetrator, one quarter reaches the witness, one quarter reaches all the members of the court, and one quarter reaches the king. (8.18)

Nor should this thought be entertained: "Whether by the plaintiff or the defendant, the land or other property of one party is seized; that person alone shall bear the fault of the seizure of land. We, however, being the ones who did not perform the act, why should we be guilty? For that sin is divided fourfold. This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), for a sin committed by one cannot pass to another. Sin arises for them as well because they have transgressed the prohibition against false perception, having a false basis. Even if the king does not see [the crime] himself, he becomes culpable due to the fault of his appointed officials, such as those acting in the capacity of the king. Or, if the king’s official, having been informed of the wrongful conduct, does not restrain the defeated wrongdoer nor provide a correct judgment, then he too becomes a partaker of the sin. Alternatively, the mention of the "king" is intended to include the official; the meaning is that when the king himself sees falsely, he is at fault, and when it is the one acting in the capacity of the king, then the fault belongs to him. (8.18)
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the assembly are released;
the guilt goes to the perpetrator where one deserving of censure is censured. (8.19)

This same point is stated by way of its converse: where one who possesses faults finds no opportunity to conceal them, and his fault is made manifest, there everything turns out well. From the verse beginning with "Where Dharma... (MDh 8.14), there follow explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) intended to show the fruits of good and evil through censure and praise, for the purpose of forbidding the neglect of false views. 8.19.
One who lives solely by his birth may indeed be called a "pseudo-Brahmin" (brāhmaṇabruva), but a Śūdra can never be the expounder of dharma to a king. (8.20)

It has been stated that one should carry out the determination of Dharma together with Brāhmaṇas and with ministers who are experts in counsel (*mantra*). Since the caste of the ministers is not specified therein, even Śūdras who have entered the assembly might—by virtue of being ministers—be authorized to determine legal proceedings; being devoted to those matters and possessing some degree of refined intellect, they might somehow express the established rules of Dharma. Furthermore, a thorough knowledge of the *Smṛti* scriptures is not required for every legal proceeding, such that the prohibition of Śūdras would be suspected of being useless on the grounds that their absence would render the matter deficient in meaning. For instance, the causes of victory and defeat—such as witnesses and so forth—are indeed to be known through worldly means of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*). One can personally discern, provided one possesses a cultivated intellect, that "this witness is righteous and has no connection to this person by any relationship," whereas "this person is not a witness because his deviation has been observed repeatedly," and so forth; this is not exclusively within the scope of the *Smṛti* scriptures. Therefore, this is a prohibition of what was otherwise applicable. Nor is there a restriction of caste regarding the office of minister, as there is for the domestic priest (*purohita*). For after stating, "He should deliberate with them" (MDh 7.56), it subsequently says, "He should deliberate with a Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 7.58). Thus, the meaning is this: even if a Śūdra should somehow acquire a slight understanding of justice, nevertheless, when litigants are disputing in the royal court, the minister or the official in charge of punishment must not say anything at all. The first half-verse of the preceding [sloka] is to be explained as a supplement to this prohibition. Indeed, it is impossible to enjoin the status of a proclaimer of Dharma upon one who lives solely by his caste and is devoid of qualities such as learning; this permission is merely a supplement to the prohibition—like the saying, "Therefore, eat poison, but do not eat in his house"—and is not a permission in its own right. For this very reason, he uses the word "kāma" (at will). For when the word "kāma" is employed, its character as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) is set aside.

Others, however, say: since the Brāhmaṇa is prescribed as the one who performs the recitation (*pravaktṛ*), it follows that at that time "the learned Brāhmaṇa should be the one appointed. Thus, the three other castes—the Kṣatriya and so forth—are excluded there. Here, however, the prohibition of the Śūdra is for the purpose of permitting the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya in the absence of a learned Brāhmaṇa. The rest is the same. In the phrase "one who lives by mere birth" (*jātimātram upajīvati*), the word *mātra* is used in the sense of restriction; he lives depending solely on the Brāhmaṇa caste itself, not on specific qualities such as Vedic study, because he is devoid of such qualities. The word *bruva* (in *brāhmaṇa-bruva*) expresses contempt. (8.20)
The kingdom of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma perishes, like a cow sinking in the mud while he looks on. (8.21)

This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) supplementary to the preceding rule: the kingdom and the subjects of that king for whom a Śūdra performs the discernment of dharma—that is, the determination of legal matters—perish and decay, like a cow in the mud. (8.21)
That kingdom which is predominantly composed of Śūdras, overrun by nihilists, and devoid of the twice-born, quickly perishes entirely, afflicted by famine and disease. (8.22)

This too is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) as before. From the context, the preponderance of *śūdras* should be understood as referring to those who decide legal disputes; that kingdom where *śūdras* constitute the majority of the adjudicators quickly perishes due to the afflictions of famine and disease. And when the kingdom perishes, the destruction of the king follows—this is what is meant. "Overrun by atheists" (*nāstikākrāntam*) is an illustration: just as [a kingdom] is overrun or occupied by atheists such as the *Lokāyatikas* and others who deny the existence of the next world, and therefore...

"Non-twice-born" (*advija*): For among atheists, the distinction between Brāhmaṇas and the other classes is not real, because of their intermingling. As it has been said: "Brāhmaṇas and the others are like the designations 'physician' or 'merchant' [which do not denote a fixed essence]. Or, in a situation where there is a conflict regarding dharma, those who are not accepted as authoritative are "non-twice-born. (8.22)
Having occupied the Dharma-seat, with his limbs properly covered and his mind composed, he should pay homage to the world-protectors and begin the examination of legal cases. (8.23)

That seat upon which *dharma* is primary is the *dharmāsana*. For on the royal throne (*rājāsana*), one makes wealth alone the primary concern, even by subordinating *dharma* in accordance with the requirements of maintaining the kingdom. However, in the determination of legal disputes, the meaning is that one should rely solely upon *dharma* as the primary factor; this does not, however, indicate a difference in the physical seat itself. *Saṃvītāṅgaḥ*: having his body covered with clothing and the like. *Praṇamya lokapālebhyah*: having paid homage to the eight world-protectors, Indra and the others; he should begin the examination of cases after having saluted them. These two acts—covering the limbs and bowing to the world-protectors—are for the sake of invisible merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). *Samāhitaḥ*: with a concentrated mind, free from distraction, during the examination of cases; for in this way, it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Alternatively, the term *samāhita* may be an adjective qualifying the act of bowing. Although it might appear here as if something has already been stated, there is no excessive redundancy because this is a metrical work (*padyagrantha*). The word *lokapālebhyaḥ* takes the dative case in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). How so? The inclusion of the "action" (*kriyā*) was enjoined in the rule concerning the recipient (*Pāṇini 1.4.32–36*), for the sake of examples such as *śrāddhāya nigṛhṇate* ("he restrains himself for the sake of the ancestral rite") and *patye śete* ("she lies down for her husband"). Furthermore, the inclusion of the "action" is not restricted only to verbs like *gṛhṇāti* ("he grasps"), as it is not so stated in the *Bhāṣya*. (8.23)
Having discerned both profit and loss, as well as merit and demerit in their entirety, he should examine all the legal cases of the litigants according to the order of their castes. (8.24)

Virtue (*dharma*) and non-virtue (*adharma*) alone are what constitute benefit (*artha*) and harm (*anartha*); the acquisition of cattle, gold, and so forth is not "benefit," nor is their opposite "harm. Rather, having understood that virtue alone is benefit and non-virtue is harm, and having resolved this in one's heart, one should examine the matters at hand. Alternatively, both benefit and harm must be understood, as well as virtue and non-virtue. One must understand the essential nature of virtue and the triviality of mere worldly benefit. Or else, where there is great harm and only a slight transgression of non-virtue, one should avoid the harm; for a slight transgression can be dispelled by means of a great benefit, such as through acts of charity or expiation. Furthermore, when many litigants are assembled, the order of the social classes (*varṇa*) should be followed. This is the sequence for the examination of classes when all are equally afflicted. However, when even a person of lower class has urgent business or a great matter, then according to the maxim "and [the case] of him whose suffering is urgent," one should examine that very case first and not respect the prescribed order. For it has been stated that the adjudication of legal disputes is for the sake of maintaining the kingdom; therefore, one should not rely solely on the literal text. (8.24)
One should discern the internal disposition of men by external signs:
by their voice, complexion, gestures, appearance, gaze, and movements. (8.25)

And thus he says this: the meaning of the verse is that even by means of inference, whether a witness speaks the truth or a falsehood must be determined according to worldly convention (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, the mention of voice (*svara*) and so forth is for the sake of illustration. By this, it is meant that one should discern [the truth] by whatever is a certain sign (*niścitaliṅga*), and not by voice and the rest alone, because those are subject to deviation (*savyabhicāritva*). For those unaccustomed to entering the court may, upon seeing the great assembly, undergo a natural transformation even if they are telling the truth. On the other hand, the bold remain with their outward appearance concealed. "Voice, complexion, and gesture" (*svaravarṇeṅgita*) refers to their "appearances" (*ākāra*); *ākāra* here means a change (*vikāra*). It is the alteration of the natural voice and so forth. By these, one should "discern," that is, determine, the "state"—meaning the internal intention—of men such as litigants and witnesses. Among these, a change in voice consists of stammering, weeping, and so on in speech; a change in complexion consists of a distortion of the body’s form and so on; a gesture (*iṅgita*) consists of perspiration, trembling, horripilation, and so on; [changes] through the eyes consist of agitation or a look of anger; and through movement (*ceṣṭita*) consists of the throwing of hands, the knitting of brows, and so on. This is self-evident (*svasaṃvedya*): that even when an intention is being hidden, the voice and other signs reveal it when observed with skill. For it is well known that these possess the power to manifest a hidden intention. (8.25)
By means of facial expressions, gestures, gait, and movements, as well as by speech and changes in the eyes and face, the mind within is perceived. (8.26)

For indeed, by this verse, [the author] demonstrates that the power [of these signs] is observed in the world through the comprehension of the meanings previously stated regarding tone of voice and so forth; thus, there is no redundancy. In this context, "modes" (*ākāra*) refers to gestures (*iṅgita*) and the like, which are performed or manifested. "Gesture" (*iṅgita*) has already been explained. The plural number is used because of the diversity of individual manifestations. "Gait" (*gati*) is an addition here compared to the previous verse. It is "stumbling," meaning altered from its natural state. "Speech" (*bhāṣita*) is discourse that contradicts its own preceding and succeeding parts. "Facial distortion" (*vaktravikāra*) refers to specific changes in the mouth and so on. The remainder has already been explained in the previous verse. The summarized meaning is: by means of these distorted worldly signs, the internal mind is perceived even in other instances. (8.26)
The king shall protect the inheritance of a minor until he has returned from his teacher's house or until he has passed his childhood. (8.27)
But surely, the administration of justice was introduced as the subject to be discussed; what, then, is the relevance of the protection of a child’s property?

It is said: this [rule] is commenced in order to exclude these very objects from being subjects of dispute: "The king shall protect the property of a minor like his own property. Otherwise, paternal uncles and other relatives would fall into dispute, each claiming, "This must be protected by me," or "This must be protected by me. Furthermore, there is no other occasion [for this rule], and because such legal proceedings might be anticipated, it is taught not merely among the duties of a king, but must therefore be stated on this very occasion. "The heir of this is a minor; that is 'the property of a minor heir' (*bāladāyādika*). Here, "heir" (*dāyāda*) refers to the owner. The king shall protect wealth owned by a minor until he has returned from the teacher's house (*samāvṛtta*), or until he has passed beyond childhood, having transcended the state of minority. And this is an alternative: for one who remains in the household during childhood, the term "passed beyond childhood" is used for that purpose. But for one who is a student (*vrataka*), even though childhood has ended, he shall have his wealth protected until his return home (*samāvartana*). Alternatively, for the twice-born (*dvijāti*), the *samāvartana* is the limit; for others, the passing of childhood is the limit. (8.27)

The same protection should be afforded to women who are barren, those whose sons are dead, those who are childless, those whose sons are incompetent, or those whose sons are destitute; likewise for women devoted to their husbands, widows, and those who are afflicted. (8.28) Whatever property belongs to anyone who is without a protector, the king shall protect it all in accordance with the law. Furthermore, the mention of "barren women" and so forth is merely illustrative; in this way, the protection of the subjects is fulfilled. The preceding verse, however, was intended to establish the temporal regulation. A *vaśā* is a barren woman. An *aputrā* is one whose sons are incapable, or one who has no sons, or one whose sons are impoverished. The term *vaśā-aputrāḥ* is a *dvandva* compound.

But is not even a barren woman without a son? True; however, both [terms, "barren" and "sonless,"] are mentioned for the sake of her protection even while her husband is alive. For when she has been superseded by another wife (*adhivinā*), the husband becomes indifferent toward her. The inclusion of the term "one whose family is extinct" (*niṣkulā*) serves as a qualification for those women who have no protector such as a brother-in-law, paternal uncle, or maternal uncle, who are themselves incapable due to their female nature, and whose kinsmen are stingy; it is for them that this is prescribed. Indeed, the character, body, and wealth of women must be protected by their kinsmen. Thus it has been said:
He is the lord over protection and maintenance;
when the husband's family is exhausted, devoid of men, and without support, he alone is the master.
"While her paternal kinsmen exist, the father’s side has authority over the woman;
but when both sides have failed, the king is the husband and has authority over the woman. (NSm 13.27–29).

However, if she herself is somehow capable [of managing her affairs], there is no role for her relatives there. For this very reason, he says: "In the case of those who are afflicted," by which incapacity is indicated.

Others, however, explain that "afflicted" refers to women whose husbands are ill; even if they are not widows, they should be protected by the king alone due to their husband's incapacity. This applies to those who have no male relatives. "Niṣkulāḥ" (those without family) refers to those who have no family or circle of kinsmen. Others, however, say that "niṣkulā" means an unchaste woman (*kulaṭā*). Even for them, wealth acquired through prostitution or other means must be protected by the king, provided they have not fallen from their caste. And in this view, the mention of "niṣkulā" includes independent women.

Regarding widows who are devoted to their husbands: a widow is one whose husband is dead; *dhava* is a name for a husband, and she is "widowed" (*vidhavā*) because she is separated from him. If she is devoted to her husband (*pativratā*), then she is [one whose] wealth must be protected. However, it is stated in another *Smṛti* that women who are addicted to adultery are unworthy of female property: "A woman who is intent on doing harm, shameless, a destroyer of wealth, and one who is addicted to adultery—she does not deserve female property."

However, her expulsion has been prescribed. And "expulsion" means placing her outside the main residence, not necessarily banishment; for even in the case of those women who have fallen [from virtue], it is ordained that they may dwell near the house and be provided with mere food and clothing:
"One should apply this same rule even to women who have fallen;
food, clothing, and drink should be given, and they should dwell near the house" (MDh 8.187).

Therefore, whatever rule regarding the disqualification of women is heard in such passages as "the woman’s property is her entire wealth," that must be understood as referring to this very same context. Nevertheless, whatever she has acquired by means of begging, spinning, and so forth, she certainly deserves that; her relatives shall not seize it. In this case, however, supersession (*ādhivedana*) is prescribed for this specific cause, but not the seizure of the woman’s property. For thus he says: "A woman who drinks liquor, is of immoral conduct, is rebellious, diseased, cruel, or constantly wasteful of wealth—she may always be superseded. (MDh 9.80)

And therefore, by the force of the *Mānava-smṛti*, this very *smṛti*—"she does not deserve [the husband's] property"—is explained as follows: she does not deserve that *strīdhana* which is given upon supersession (*ādhivedanika*); the meaning is that it should not be given to her. As for what was stated: "One should give an equal amount as *ādhivedanika* to a woman who has been superseded" (YDh 2.152), it does not mean that what was previously given to her must be taken away.
We, however, say: the forfeiture is indeed appropriate in the case of a woman who hates her husband or is addicted to adultery; for it is also stated here: [text continues].
"She who transgresses against one who is negligent, intoxicated, or afflicted by disease shall be abandoned for three months, deprived of her ornaments and belongings. (MDh 9.78).
The meaning is that she must be made destitute of her ornaments and personal effects. 8.28.
But if their own kinsmen should seize the property of those women while they are still alive, a righteous lord of the earth should punish them with the punishment due to thieves. 8.29.

This is the punishment for thieves applied to kinsmen who misappropriate the property of women; for they misappropriate it through various fraudulent means. [The king should think: "This woman is not her own master; what can she give, or what can she enjoy? We are the masters here. Thus, out of fear that they might be suspected of being non-thieves, the punishment for thieves is ordained. While those women are still living, the king should punish—that is, restrain—those kinsmen, such as brothers-in-law and others, who seize their wealth. The punishment for thieves will be described [later]: "With whatever limb a thief commits an offense against men..."
"That which ought to be cut off, that very thing [must be done], for that is the instruction of Manu. (MDh 8.334).
This must be protected by the king especially from his own kinsmen; however, protection against thieves is prescribed as pertaining to one's own kingdom. 8.29.
The king shall cause property whose owner has disappeared to be kept in custody for three years;
within three years the owner may take it, but after that time the king may take it himself. 8.30

If a certain object belonging to an owner has been lost through negligence while traveling on a road and dropped somewhere, whether in a forest or a wilderness, and is found by forest-keepers or other royal officials and brought before the king, the king shall provide protection for it and place it publicly at the palace gate or on the royal highway. Alternatively, it should be announced by the sounding of a drum, proclaiming: "Whose [property] is this that was lost? It must be kept under the supervision of guards in the very place where it was found. It should remain there for three years. Within those three years, whoever can prove it is his own by means of evidence shall be granted the share to be recovered—consisting of the sixth part and so forth—as will be described later; after that period, it shall be entered into the king’s own treasury.

That property whose owner has disappeared is "pranaṣṭasvāmika" (ownerless). "Pranaṣṭa" means unknown; "riktha" means wealth. The compound "tryabdam" is a collective term for three years (*trayāṇām abdānāṃ samāhāraḥ*). Just as in the case of *trivarṣa*, there is an absence of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* in *tryabda*. The word *abda* is a synonym for *saṃvatsara* (year). "Nidhāpayet" means he should cause it to be placed [in custody]. "Arvāk tryabdāt" means prior to three years; the owner may take possession before the three years have elapsed. The word *arvāk* denotes a limit and signifies "before" in terms of direction, space, and so forth.

Others, however, say that the phrase "the king may take it" is a permission for enjoyment and not an act of seizure; for it is not proper to seize the property of another even after three years have passed. Therefore, if the owner does not appear after three years, the king may enjoy the property.

How should this verse be explained by them: "Whatever [property] for ten years... (MDh 8.147)? If it is argued that the seizure of another's property is improper, then possession (*bhoga*) is likewise not proper; for another's property, when being used like clothing and such, is indeed destroyed. In that case, the figurative treatment of it as "not seized" would be appropriate, since the very act of using it constitutes the result of seizure. However, one must state what kind of "possession" there can be in the case of elephants, horses, and the like. Therefore, there is no reason to abandon the literal meaning of the text. Furthermore, the root *harati* is frequently seen used in the sense of "to take" or "to acquire," as in "he shall take the inheritance" (*ṛkthaṃ haret*) and so forth. Consequently, the meaning is simply this: the king should "seize"—that is, take possession of—it from the other. (8.30)
But how, then, can an owner establish his ownership when the property has been lost? To this he says:
"He who says, 'This is mine,' shall be questioned according to the rule;
having verified the form, number, and other details, the owner deserves that property. (8.31)

Whoever comes and says, "This is my own property," he should be interrogated according to the prescribed rule. "Interrogated" means he should be questioned. What is this method of interrogation? "Who are you? What property was lost? Of what appearance, what size, what number, was it? Was it fallen or not fallen? If it was fallen, in what place? Likewise, from where was it obtained by you? In this manner, the interrogation must be conducted. If he corroborates the appearance, the number, and so forth—where "appearance" refers to living beings, clothing, and the like, such as "a white garment" or "a cow"—and likewise the "number," such as "ten cows" or "yokes," and by the inclusion of "and so forth," the measurement of hands and the like, the quantity of gold and the like, or its miscellaneous form—if he corroborates all of this, then he is the owner. Therefore, he is entitled to take that property for himself. Corroboration is said to occur when whatever has been determined by one person through a particular means of knowledge is determined by this person in exactly the same way. And the mention of "appearance, number, and so forth" is for the sake of illustration, as there are other grounds for ownership, such as witnesses and the like. (8.31)
One who fails to report accurately the place and time of the lost item,
as well as its color, form, and size, deserves a fine equal to that of the value of the object.

This penalty is prescribed for one who acts falsely: he who does not declare the place and time of the lost property—stating whether it was lost in this place or at this time—nor its true nature or ultimate reality, such as its color (white and so forth), its form (a cloth, a pair of garments, and so forth), or its measurement (five cubits in length, seven cubits in measure, and so forth); then, being untruthful regarding that matter, he deserves a fine equal to that, being equivalent to the amount of wealth concerning which he acted falsely. (8.32)
Then, remembering the duty of the virtuous, the king should take a sixth, a tenth, or even a twelfth part of goods lost and then recovered. (8.33)

He should take—that is, he should seize—a sixth, a tenth, or a twelfth part of the property found after it was lost. He should hand over the remainder to the owner. In this regard, a twelfth part is taken in the first year, a tenth in the second, and a sixth in the third. Alternatively, the choice of share depends on the degree of effort and trouble involved in guarding the property. This is done by one who remembers the dharma of the virtuous and recognizes that this is the established practice of the learned. (8.33)
Property that has been lost and subsequently found shall remain under the supervision of appointed officials;
whatever thieves the king may catch there, he shall have them executed by an elephant.

"Recovered after being lost" means that which was previously lost and subsequently recovered. It should be kept under the supervision of appointed and diligent guards. Even if it remains thus protected, should some thieves seize it, the king shall have them slain by an elephant (*ibha*, i.e., *hastin*). The mention of the "elephant" is for the sake of an unseen [spiritual] merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). (8.34)
If a man should truthfully declare, "This treasure is mine," the king may take a sixth or even a twelfth part of it. (8.35)

Wealth deposited secretly in the ground is called a *nidhi* (treasure-trove). Such treasures may be hundreds or even thousands of years old. If, while the earth is being excavated, a treasure-trove is somehow discovered by someone, that belongs to the king. Thus says Gautama: "The discovery of a treasure-trove is the property of the king" (GDh 10.43). This rule is to be understood as applying to a treasure whose depositor is not remembered; in that case, it is stated that "the person who reports it shall receive a sixth part. However, this verse should be seen as referring to cases where the depositor himself, or his agent, or his ancestors such as a father or grandfather, is known. The meaning is: "He who says, 'This treasure is mine,' should prove it by truthful evidence. "He shall take a sixth part of it": once its ownership has been established, the king takes a sixth or other portion. The choice of share depends on the qualities of the informant. (8.35)
But one who speaks falsely shall be fined an eighth part of his own wealth, or a smaller fraction of the value of that very deposit. 8.36.

But he who does not prove his claim that "this treasure was deposited by me" or "by my ancestor" is a liar and shall be punished. He shall be made to pay an eighth part of whatever wealth he possesses, or rather, a smaller fraction, portion, or share of that very treasure—this is the meaning. However, one should not compel him to give back that specific substance, such as gold and so forth; rather, one should impose a fine of that same quantity or another of equal value, by means of which amount of wealth the punished person will not fall into ruin and may be brought to submission. A choice between these options should be adopted depending on specific circumstances such as the consequences (*anubandha*) and the qualities of the individual. This indicates that the fine is less than the previous maximum penalty. Therefore, if a man has great wealth but the treasure is small, he should be fined an eighth part of his total wealth in consideration of the treasure; for that [eighth part of his wealth] would be a much smaller amount. (8.36)
But a learned Brāhmaṇa, having discovered a treasure previously deposited, may take it entirely, for he is the master of all. (8.37)

[140] When a learned Brāhmaṇa discovers a treasure deposited by his ancestors, such as his father and others, he may take it all; he need not give to the king the share previously mentioned. This is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*): for he is the master of everything. And so it has been said: "All this is the property of the Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 1.100). This taking of the whole applies only when the treasure belongs to a Brāhmaṇa. However, in the case of a treasure whose owner is unknown, the king's share certainly exists even when it is found by a learned Brāhmaṇa; for the author will state later: "But of ancient treasures... (MDh 8.39). [8.37]
But whatever ancient treasure a king may discover buried in the earth, he should give half of it to the twice-born and deposit the other half in his treasury. (8.38)

This is the king’s ordinance for the distribution of this treasure to the Brahmins from that treasure which was discovered by the king himself. By the word *kośa*, a place for the accumulation of wealth is meant. "Laid up of old in the earth" is a descriptive restatement of its nature as a treasure (*nidhi*). (8.38)
For the king is the lord of the earth; he receives half the share of the ancient treasures and minerals found in the ground because of his duty to protect them. (8.39)

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) for the previously mentioned rule that even when a treasure-trove is found by someone other than the king, the king must take his share: "For of ancient treasures... and so forth. And regarding "minerals in the earth": this is an injunction for what was not previously established. "Minerals" (*dhātavaḥ*) are the seeds of gold, silver, and the like, as well as red lead, black ointment, and so on. Whoever digs into the ground where gold and other minerals are produced, or whoever makes a living from minerals such as red chalk (*gairika*) on mountains and the like, must likewise give a share to the king as before.
