Regarding the term *ardhabhāga*: the word *ardha* here denotes a mere portion because it is used in a compound, just as in the expressions "half a village" (*grāmārdha*) or "half a city" (*nagarārdha*). Although the neuter gender usually indicates an equal division, in this case—because no specific gender distinction is understood within the compound, because of the force of the preceding word "and" (*ca*), and because a share of six, ten, twelve, or more is the subject under discussion—it is understood to denote that [specific] share. The meaning is: he takes a part, he seizes a portion. The reason for this is stated: "Because of protection. Even though royal protection may not be required for what is buried in the earth since no one knows of it, nevertheless, its seizure by a powerful person is possible. Therefore, protection is indeed purposeful. For this very reason, he says: "For he is the lord of the earth. He is the master of the earth; and it is proper that a share be given to him of whatever is obtained from that land belonging to him. (8.39)
The king must restore to all classes the wealth stolen by thieves;
by using that for himself, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. (8.40)

Whatever wealth has been taken by thieves, the king, having recovered it, should not appropriate it for himself. Rather, it must be restored to those very persons who were robbed. By the use of the word "all," it is implied that it should be given even to *caṇḍālas*. Regarding the alternative reading "caurāhṛtam": having analyzed it as "that which was brought (*āhṛtam*) by thieves (*cauraiḥ*)," the compound is formed according to Pāṇini 2.1.32, *kṛtā*. In the other reading, "caurahṛtam," the compound is formed either by the previous rule or by the application of the *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) from Pāṇini 2.1.30, *tṛtīyā*. However, the meaning here is this: whatever has been carried off by thieves and cannot be recovered, that must be provided by the king from his own treasury.

The second half of the verse should be construed as follows: "the king, making use of that. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *yuj* preceded by the prefix *upa* should be understood here as meaning "to appropriate" through metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇā*). For when someone does not give wealth to another when the time for it has arrived, but instead employs it for his own purposes, it is rightly said that he has made use of it as if it were his own: "The king, making use of that, incurs the guilt of the thief. *Kilbiṣa* means sin (*pāpa*). (8.40)
One who knows the law, having carefully considered the laws of castes and regions, the laws of guilds, and the laws of families, should establish the specific duty (svadharma) for each. 8.41.

Countries such as Kurukṣetra, Piṣṭapura, and Kaśmīra, having fixed boundaries, constitute a *janapada* (region). The customs (*dharma*) existing therein are called *jānapada*. Some [customs] exist there which are practiced under the specific designations of those regions. Alternatively, the people residing there are designated by the word *janapada*, according to the maxim "the platforms cry out" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*). The customs to be performed by them are *jānapada*. The secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.129 (*tasyedam*). The genitive compound *jāter jānapadā jātijānapadāḥ* means "local customs pertaining to a particular class. Local customs that concern only a specific class must be protected by the king. Having examined and deliberated—whether they are contrary to the sacred scriptures (*āmnāya*) or not, and likewise whether they cause harm to anyone or not—the king should establish and cause to be practiced those that are not contrary; this is the meaning. And so he will say later: "That which is practiced by the virtuous... (MDh 8.46).

Alternatively, it is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "those who are both inhabitants of the land and [belonging to] a caste. By the word "caste" (*jāti*), permanence is indicated. This is merely a way of praising the local customs (*deśadharma*): just as a caste is eternal, so too are the local customs—provided they do not contradict the scriptures—eternal. These, such as the grazing of cattle and the flow of water, must be observed as if they were permanent, even when their purpose is visible. For example, villagers might establish an agreement that "cattle are not to be grazed in this area" for the sake of accomplishing some task; whoever violates that rule there is to be punished by the king.

Alternatively, those who exist in a *janapada* (country) are called *jānapadas*, meaning inhabitants of a region. *Jātijānapadas* are those who are by birth *jānapadas*. "Birth" (*jāti*) means, in short, origin or production. By this, the permanence of the connection between persons and the country is indicated. Those who are born in that country, whose ancestors were born in that country, and who reside there—those who are qualified by all these attributes, and whose qualities have existed from time immemorial (*anidaṃprathamataḥ*), are designated by the term *jātijānapada*. Although the secondary suffix *cha* would have been expected according to Pāṇini 4.2.114 (*vṛddhāc chaḥ*), the suffix *aṇ* has been used instead due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*).

Alternatively, by way of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), the word "person" (*puruṣa*) is applied to the qualities (*dharma*) associated with him. Therefore, this restriction of place regarding these qualities is to be understood as originating from such a person. For these are the local customs (*deśadharma*) of the barbarians (*mleccha*), and not those of the Āryas. They, possessing characteristics similar to animals, are not entitled to [the Vedic rites] elsewhere; they practice customs established by their own tradition, such as marrying their mothers and so forth. This [practice] is not to be prohibited by a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*). Since this is a law of their caste (*jātidharma*), it is permitted because of their connection to living in that particular country; furthermore, there is no contradiction with the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) here, for contradiction applies only to those who are entitled [to the Veda], not to animals.

But is it not the case that [the qualities of] "non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, purity, and restraint of the senses" (MDh 10.63) were stated specifically with reference to those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*)? And the Mlecchas are indeed those born in the inverse order. Therefore, if one is not at fault for marrying a mother or for the absence of purification by water after voiding urine, what would constitute restraint of the senses, or what kind of purity would there be?

This has been stated: these duties, such as purity and the rest, pertain to those residing in the heart of Āryāvarta; however, there is no restriction of duties to specific regions for the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*). We shall explain later that some regional customs (*deśadharma*) have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Guilds, artisans, laborers, chariot-warriors, and the like have entered into a common purpose; their rules are *śreṇī-dharma* (guild laws). For example, certain merchant leaders, by verbal agreement, deliver to the king his fixed share [of profit], saying: "We live by this trade; this is your royal share, while whatever profit remains shall be ours—whether it be less or more. Once the king has accepted the trade, they establish mutual regulations for the sake of exceeding the profit, which may involve opposition to the state, such as: "This commodity must not be sold for such a length of time," or "This fine falls upon us under the pretext of the king," or "It is for the sake of a festival for the deity. In that case, if anyone transgresses, he is to be punished for violating the guild law (*śreṇī-dharma*).

"Family laws" (*kuladharma*) refers to the family lineage (*kula* or *vaṃśa*). Within that lineage, a law is established by an ancestor of renowned greatness, such as: "Any member born of our lineage who obtains wealth from any source shall not employ it for any purpose other than giving it to Brahmins," and so forth. Likewise, provided there is suitability, those very persons who were the officiating priests (*yājaka*) of one's ancestors, or those to whom they gave their daughters in marriage and the like, must be employed. One who transgresses this should be compelled by the king to perform it. These are mentioned again because, since they involve a collective body of people, there might be a suspicion that they are contrary to *dharma*; we shall explain later that this is not a case of violating a private agreement (*saṃvidvyatikrama*). (8.41)
Performing their own duties and remaining steadfast in their respective tasks, men become dear to the world even when they are far away. (8.42)

By this verse, the visible and invisible nature of the previously mentioned duties of the local community and so forth is demonstrated. Those who perform their own duties in accordance with the traditions of their family become dear even when they are far away; whereas everyone else becomes dear because of proximity and excessive association. However, one who performs his own duty remains dear even while staying at a distance. By the phrase "established in their respective duties," the non-performance of the duties of others is expressed. The meaning of the verse is that those who do not perform the work of others become dear to all. (8.42)
The king himself should not initiate a legal case, nor should his official;
nor should he ever swallow up a matter brought forward by another. (8.43)

A *kārya* is the subject matter of a dispute. The king shall not initiate such a case himself for the purpose of harming some seditious person or for the purpose of seizing the wealth of a wealthy man; he must not harass that man’s debtor or anyone else who has offended him by saying: "Why do you not drag this man before me, since he owes you this? or "This man has committed such an offense that I shall have him executed"—the king must not act in this way, even if he feels hatred or greed for wealth. Nor should he "swallow" (*graset*) what has been brought forward and reported by another plaintiff—that is, he should not suppress it. The verb *nigirati* is used in the sense of disregard, and *grasati* has the same meaning. Thus people say: "Whatever is said to him, he swallows it all; he does not answer anything."

Others, however, explain the latter half of the verse as follows: "And he shall not seize—that is, take possession of—the wealth or property that has been brought forward by means other than through legal procedure (*vyavahāra*). For if the king were to proceed with a monetary fine based on even a slight pretext of fraud, then a fault would be seen in the next world, and there would be ruin within his own kingdom."

Now, there is this other interpretation by some: the king should not initiate a legal case himself. Even if he perceives directly someone committing an improper act, he should not say anything himself until he has been drawn into the judicial process by the defendant. This is so that the mere observation of the lawsuit serves for the punishment of the defeated party, and not the king himself. And this rule is to be understood as applying only to cases such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) and the like. However, those who are like "thorns"—such as thieves, violent offenders, and the like—the king should apprehend them himself once he has discovered them. The rest is the same.
Nor is he "the man" (puruṣa) of this king; that is, he is not the authorized human servant of this king. 8.43.
Just as a hunter traces the track of a deer by drops of blood, so should a king trace the path of dharma by means of inference. 8.44

As it has been said: "Even though he has seen [an offense] himself, a king should not suddenly attack or punish anyone, for this may occur even in jest. How, then, is this to be understood—whether this was done in jest or was prompted by anger and other such motives? To this he says: "This is to be known through inference (*anumāna*). Just as a hunter, having struck a deer that has vanished from his sight, tracks and reaches its trail by means of drops of blood flowing from a wound, so too should a king determine the cause of a matter, whether it be out of his sight or within his direct perception, by means of inference. And *dharma* is the realization of the truth regarding the subject matter of legal proceedings. The repetition of what has already been stated regarding inference is for the sake of strengthening the memory. (8.44)
Established in the procedure of legal proceedings, he should carefully examine the truth, the matter at hand, himself as the witness, the place, the appearance, and the time. (8.45)

Established and engaged in the procedure of legal proceedings—that is, in the business of litigation—one should not merely examine the words of the lawsuit, but also these other factors, beginning with truth.

In that regard, the perception of truth is as follows: even if neither the plaintiff nor the defendant, out of modesty, has stated the matter with complete words, if the king is somehow able to determine—through other means of proof or through the aforementioned inference—that "the matter is such," then he should rely upon that and not disregard it on the grounds that "this person has not stated everything. As it has been said: "Having set aside deception, the king should conduct legal proceedings according to the facts" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.19).

"Seeing the matter" (*arthasya darśanam*): the word *artha* here signifies either "wealth" or "purpose. In that regard, if one should obtain a great matter, then even having set aside other royal duties, one should not be distressed; one must indeed attend to the examination of the legal case. Alternatively, if someone should say, "The matter was taken from this person by witnesses or by another member of the court," then it must be investigated whether this subject of litigation is so small that the seizure of wealth is impossible. If, however, the members of the court and the witnesses have fallen into distress, then it should be considered probable and determined through other means of proof.

And this should be investigated by making oneself the witness. This is what is meant: one should employ spies according to the logic of "weeding out thorns. Alternatively, one should observe oneself—that is, one should observe one's own condition—whether there is a depletion of the treasury or an abundance of great wealth. In this interpretation, the word *sākṣin* (witness) is an independent term. Regarding the observation of place: in some instances even a small matter attains greatness, while that which is great elsewhere may become insignificant in a certain place; such is the observation of place. Time, too, should be viewed in the same way.
Form has the nature of being an object of conventional usage; one should perceive its heaviness or lightness.

Others, however, have explained it as follows: one should perceive the essence and the fruit in truth and wealth, making oneself the witness. This is what is meant: because truth is weightier due to its great purpose, and because it serves as the means for achieving both worlds, truth must be resorted to; wealth, on the other hand, is to be abandoned because of its lack of essence. "Place" refers to heaven and so forth, which is attainable by resorting to truth. "Time" refers to dwelling there for a long duration. "Form" refers to a beautiful, handsome, and captivating appearance. The opposite of this results from abandoning truth and resorting solely to wealth. (8.45)

Whatever has been practiced by the virtuous and by righteous twice-born men, that he should establish as the law for regions, families, and castes, provided it is not in conflict with [the sacred tradition]. (8.46)

The *santaḥ* (the peaceful) are those who avoid what is prohibited; the *dhārmikāḥ* (the righteous) are those who perform what is enjoined. Although a single word is capable of conveying both meanings, nevertheless, because they are presented as distinct, they are explained thus by way of distinguishing their respective domains. Whatever they practice that is not found in the words of the revealed *Śruti* or the traditional *Smṛti*, one should establish—that is, cause to be performed—for regions, families, and castes, provided it is not in conflict with the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* as they are currently available. Regarding what was stated in the verse, "the laws of castes and regions" (*jātijānapadān dharmān*, MDh 8.41), the authority of the customs of regions, families, and so forth was established there; here, a specific qualification of that is being stated: such [customs] are authoritative when there is no contradiction with the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), but they are not authoritative when there is a contradiction. Consequently, even village, regional, or royal affairs that serve visible purposes (*dṛṣṭārtha*) are to be respected if they do not contradict the scriptures, but not if they do. For example, in some regions, a debtor is made to pay a debt by selling himself; however, that contradicts the rule: "even by labor" (*karmaṇāpi samam*, MDh 8.177). Another point is shown by the verse. As for other custom, its authority is stated precisely through its connection with the *śiṣṭas* (the refined): "and the conduct of the virtuous" (*ācāraś caiva sādhūnām*, MDh 2.6). And goodness (*sādhutva*) is not possible through the performance of practices contrary to that [scriptural authority]. Therefore, this instruction refers to matters that do not pertain to the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).

But another says: In another region, whatever is practiced by righteous and virtuous twice-born men that is not contradicted by the Śruti or by another Smṛti, the King should ordain that even in other regions. For example, the *udvṛṣabhayajña* and other such rites, well-known among the Northerners (*udīcya*), should be performed by those of the East, the South, and the West. Why? Because from practice (*ācāra*) a Smṛti must be inferred, and from Smṛti the Śruti. And if that [Smṛti] were inferred as "this should be done by the Northerners," then—since the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is recorded in memory as having many meanings, such as "born there" (Pāṇini 4.3.25), "existing there" (Pāṇini 4.3.53), "come from there" (Pāṇini 4.3.74), and "set out toward that" (Pāṇini 4.3.89)—and because this suffix possesses both the nature of a characteristic and a modification, and since the suffix is remembered for other meanings not explicitly mentioned for each term, there is no such thing as a "Northerner" who could be excluded by the word "udīcya. Consequently, it follows that this [practice] must be performed by any person whatsoever, because a designation of place lacks a fixed cause and is therefore non-restrictive. If, on the other hand, the sentence were inferred thus: "by one born in the North, or by an inhabitant of that region," that too is inconsistent. For one born there does not perform it elsewhere, and an inhabitant of that region who was born elsewhere certainly does not perform it either. If one says, "one whose lineage is from the Northern region and who is an inhabitant of that region," that too is not tenable because of the impermanence of lineage and residence; for residence and lineage are not permanent like caste, quality, or clan. Therefore, since no permanent differentiator of performers can be established, all *dharma*s have universal scope. There are no such things as "regional *dharmas*" (*deśadharma*). By this same logic, "family *dharmas*" (*kuladharma*) are also explained.

How then is it that the authors of the *Smṛtis* designate them separately as "the laws of regions (*deśadharma*)" and "the laws of families (*kuladharma*)"? It has been stated that these are fixed arrangements based on perceptible purposes; in that regard, it was explained that both the *dharma* and its restriction (*niyama*) are appropriate. Furthermore, a family (*kula*) is a subset of a lineage (*gotra*). As for that which is the *dharma* of an entire lineage—such as "Vasiṣṭhas should not intermarry with Vaiśvāmitras"—because the designation of a lineage is eternal, that [law] is indeed eternal; thus, we shall desist from further discussion. (8.46)
That which is common to all titles of legal procedure has been stated. Now, with the intention of specifying a particular case, he says this:
"When urged by the creditor for the sake of recovering his debt from the debtor, the king shall cause the creditor to receive the amount proved from the debtor. (8.47)

"He who takes money from another with the thought, 'I shall repay it with interest at a later time,' is the debtor (*adhamarṇa*). He who employs [the money] with the thought, 'I shall recover it with interest,' is the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). These two are relative terms. The meaning of *adhamarṇa* is *artha*. *Artha* means wealth; by virtue of the context, that which is to be given to the creditor is what is expressed here. Its accomplishment (*siddhi*) is its delivery to the creditor. The second word *artha* expresses purpose. This is the collective meaning: when the creditor is urged by the king, saying, 'May the wealth that was taken by the debtor be accomplished for me; may Your Majesty, the King, cause it to be paid,' then the King should cause the creditor's wealth to be paid by the debtor. One who possesses wealth is a *dhanika*; by common usage, the creditor alone is called *dhanika*. Because of the connection with the verb 'should cause to pay' (*dāpayet*), the dative case would have been expected, but it is not used because the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is incomplete. For example, in expressions such as 'he gives his back to the one who strikes him' or 'he gives the garment to the washerman,' the primary sense of 'giving' is not present. Here too, since ownership exists for both [in the case of the former] and ownership is absent for both [in the case of the latter], the sense of 'giving' is incomplete."

Is he to be made to pay solely on the word of the creditor? No, it says: "when it has been proven. This means when it is established by certain evidence that he owes the debt. Alternatively, "proven" (*vibhāvita*) means he has admitted it himself; for the author will later state regarding one who denies it: "in the case of the debtor's denial" (MDh 8.52). But how can one who has admitted it himself be called "proven"? This is not a fault. For in the event of forgetfulness, one becomes "admitted" by means of a document in one's own hand and so forth; yet one may be "proven" while not admitting it, being one who knows [the truth] but falsely denies it. (8.47)
By whatever means a creditor may recover his own wealth, by those very means he should constrain the debtor and compel him to pay. 8.48.

In this world, a creditor will not demand his share from the king for a debt not yet paid, nor will he pay a fine for a debt already settled. In such a situation, out of greed for their own share, kings might cause creditors to seek wealth through improper means; therefore, this is stated to prevent that. By whichever of the methods to be described hereafter the creditor may recover his own wealth previously lent, by those very means he should compel the debtor to pay. *Saṃgṛhya* means having restrained or stabilized [the debtor]; the sense is that he should act after determining, "By this specific method, this amount can be obtained from him. Alternatively, *saṃgraha* refers to conciliation (*upasāntvana*) that is favorable. The term *uttamarṇika* refers to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*). That which is supreme (*uttama*) and is a debt (*ṛṇa*) is *uttamarṇa*; one who possesses that is *uttamarṇika*. The form is derived according to Pāṇini 5.2.115 (*ata iniṭhanau*). The same applies to the other two terms (*madhyamarṇika* and *adhamarṇika*). In compounds such as *sarvadhanika*, the suffix should be applied; otherwise, as in the expression "a village with brave men" (*vīrapuruṣaka*), the compound is formed as a *bahuvrīhi* because of grammatical coreferentiality, since there is no difference in meaning between the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) and the stated sense. Furthermore, the possessive suffix is difficult to apply here. Debt (*ṛṇa*) is wealth placed under a transaction for the sake of interest or profit. It has two related parties: the lender and the borrower. For the lender, it is "supreme" (*uttama*) because he is independent in both giving the money and receiving it back. For the other, it is "inferior" (*adhama*) because he gives with an increase [of interest] and because of the great effort involved. However, this is merely an etymological derivation; in common usage, these two terms are simply designations for the lender and the borrower. The following verse is intended to demonstrate what those methods are. (8.48)
One should recover a debt that has been lent through legal process, through trickery, through customary practice, and by force as the fifth means. (8.49)

In this regard, according to the method of the *Dharmaskandha*, there is a gradual taking [of wealth]: "This today, this tomorrow, this the day after tomorrow; just as the maintenance of a household is for him, so too are we members of your family, worthy of sharing"—such is the practice of *dharma* as recited in the texts. However, one who is destitute should be made to pay through legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*). In other cases, having given money like water poured into the ear, he should be made to engage in trade, agriculture, and so forth; the wealth produced therein should be taken from him. But as for a legal proceeding that must be reported to the king, because it involves the employment of all possible means and because it is undertaken by the application of force (*balagrahaṇa*), [one may take it]. Furthermore, one who does not give directly even though possessing wealth should be made to pay through artifice. Under some pretext, such as a wedding or festival, one should take ornaments like bracelets and not return them until that wealth has been paid by him. Artifice includes fasting, sitting at the door of the house, and so on. Force is appearing before the king's court. There, the king, having restrained and pressured one who does not give through conciliation, makes him pay. However, "force" does not refer to wealth related to one's own household, because in this very context Uśanas states: "The king is the force of the subjects."

Others, however, explain that this instruction is intended for the king alone, because it occurs within the section on the duties of kings (*rājadharmaprakaraṇa*). Once informed by [the judge] of the means [to recover his debt], the king should cause the defeated debtor—who has either been won over or has surrendered himself—to pay. However, he must not forcibly seize all of his property and hand it over to the creditor at once; for the king must act so as to favor both parties. If the entire property were given away, the debtor’s family would be ruined, and that too is improper. For it has been said: "He should not be harassed; rather, he should be made to pay gradually, from time to time, according to his income."

"But especially so when the king is righteous," [says the law]. Therefore, he should be made to pay something by way of interest; if there is an abundance of wealth beyond what is required for his family, he should be made to pay everything. And if nothing at all is available, [the rule applies]: "He should make him equal [to the debt] even by labor" (MDh 8.177). According to another interpretation, deceitful conduct and improper behavior should not be employed without first informing the king. 8.49.
If a creditor recovers his own wealth from a debtor by his own means, he must not be prosecuted by the king for recovering what is his own. (8.50)

This verse is intended to clarify the very point already stated: when a creditor is recovering his money from a debtor by means other than *chala* (fraudulent artifice) and so forth, acting according to his own will, he must not be addressed by the king with any such words as: "Why have you taken ornaments and other property from him under a pretext or through deception for the purpose of clearing your own debt, without informing me? Or, having taken it, why do you not return it to him? (8.50)

But when the debtor is unable to pay the debt, yet the cause [of his inability] has been clearly demonstrated, the judge shall cause him to pay the amount due to the creditor and a small fine according to his capacity. (8.51)

Even when there exists a means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the truth, one should not employ deceptive tactics (*chala*) against a person who does not admit it of his own accord. Rather, the king himself must be informed of the matter. When the case has been brought before the king, if a debtor denies a debt—saying, "I owe him nothing"—and is subsequently established by evidence consisting of witnesses, documents, or possession as having indeed owed the debt, the king should compel him to pay the money to the creditor. He should also impose a small fine, meaning merely a token fine. Elsewhere, he will prescribe a tenth part [of the debt]. However, one who is unable to pay that much should be made to pay even a small fine, less than a tenth part. Alternatively, this fine of less than a tenth part is for one who, through negligence or some form of forgetfulness, denies the claim; it is a penalty according to his capacity. Evidence (*kāraṇa*) is a means of proof (*pramāṇa*), and it is of three kinds. These are enumerated here because they are possible in this context. And so they say:
"Where there is no written document, nor is a witness found, and the aforementioned proof is absent, there the divine mode of proof shall prevail. (8.51)
When a debtor, being addressed with "Give! in the presence of an assembly, denies the debt, the plaintiff must point out the place [of the transaction] or state another reason. (8.52)

When, in an assembly or a court of law presided over by a king or a judge, there occurs through unrighteous means the denial or concealment of one who has been told, "Give the debt to the creditor," then the complainant—the creditor who advanced the money—should "indicate the place" (*diśet*), that is, point out a witness who serves as proof; or he should indicate another "cause," such as a written document (*lekhyādi*). By the word "place" (*deśa*), those witnesses residing in the location where the loan was made are figuratively included; thus, although the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is a general term, like the expression "cattle and bulls" (*gobalīvarda*), it denotes causes other than witnesses, such as written documents. Consequently, there is an alternative reading: "or he should state the cause" (*kāraṇaṃ vā samuddiśet*); the meaning of this is exactly the same.

Alternatively, there is this other reading: "The accused shall point out the place. This is its meaning: when a debtor, upon being told "Give [the debt]," admits, "It is true that the money was indeed returned," he who was previously the plaintiff has now become the defendant. That defendant shall point out the place: "In what place was it returned by you to me? He shall also specify the time, since the mention of "place" is intended to be illustrative. Or, he shall state the reason: "Sir, is there a reason for your repayment? Point that out. Thus he should speak. Alternatively, he shall point out the "place of proof" (*deśya*): namely, whether at that time witnesses and so forth were shown, or what the reason was. The word *vā* (or) is used in place of the word *ca* (and). (8.52)
He who points out an improper direction, and he who, having pointed it out, retracts it; and he who does not understand the meanings of what precedes and follows when they are contradictory—(8.53)

It has already been stated that when a debtor denies a debt, the creditor must inform the king; and the notification should be made in this manner: "In this place and at this time, this much wealth was received from me by him. If, when questioned, he asserts, "I was not in this place at the time of the receipt specified by him," then he points to an incorrect location (*adeśa*). Alternatively, witnesses have been described; he points to those witnesses as being impossible regarding the place and time. Having pointed out the place and so forth, he then disavows it, saying, "This was not pointed out by me. Furthermore, he who does not understand the points of the case—both the preceding and the subsequent, the earlier and the later—which have been stated in a confused or contradictory manner; or who says later what should have been said earlier, and says earlier what should have been said later, and does not keep track of his own deviation from the proper sequence of speech—"he is defeated," one should declare him to be so. The verb [to be declared] will apply everywhere [in the following]. (MDh 8.57) || 8.53 ||
Furthermore, he who, having stated and restated his case, then evades it;
or who, when questioned, does not accept a matter that has been correctly established. (8.54)

The first half [of the verse] provides a conclusion to the matter already stated; the second half states a matter not yet mentioned. That which was stated in the verse, "He who points out a wrong place, and he who, having pointed it out, denies it" (MDh 8.53), is precisely the meaning of the term *apadiśya*. A *deśa* (place) that is improper is itself an *apadeśa* (pretext). Having *apadiśya*—that is, having declared—that [wrong place], he subsequently flees or retreats, saying later: "These two, place and time, were not determined by me; this belongs to me only for as long as one fixes upon a place and time. He, too, is deprived of that object.

When one has correctly formulated a point that is coherent and certain, yet when questioned about it, one does not provide a response—being asked, "What do you say to this? or "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do you establish your own position?"—and instead shifts the subject, thinking, "I will delay the time, for I shall surely suffer defeat at the conclusion of the investigation," then he too suffers defeat. Alternatively, one who uses a pretext (*apadeśa*), which is a subterfuge, and having put forward that pretext, withdraws, saying, "A great affliction has now arisen for me; I am unable to reply," or one who proceeds with falsehoods and the like, also loses. (8.54)
He who converses secretly with witnesses in a place where conversation is forbidden, he who does not wish to answer when being questioned, or he who flees from the court; 8.55.

In a place unfit for conversation, such as a secluded corner (*upahvara*) and the like, he converses with the witnesses alone, fearing that they might break ranks. When being interrogated, questioned, or examined, he refuses to address the inquiry or the matter under investigation; he gains time by citing some royal business or by seeking the favor of the king’s sons, ministers, and others. And as for him who “should flee”—the verb to be supplied is precisely what will be stated later: “he loses” (*sa hīyate*, MDh 8.56). The meaning of “he who should flee” (*yaś cāpi niṣpatet*) is the same as that which was already mentioned in “but he who runs away again” (*punar yas tv apadhāvati*, MDh 8.54). Since a purpose for this repetition has been stated—namely, so that there may not be excessive redundancy (*atyantapaunaruktya*)—some distinction must be maintained. (8.55)
If, when told "Speak," he does not speak, or if he fails to clarify what has been said, or if he cannot distinguish the sequence of what precedes and follows, he is defeated on that point. (8.56)

This very verse, whose meaning has already been stated, is seen here again through other verses; and the purpose for repeating it has been explained: "That which is beneficial should be understood even many times. As for the literal meaning: when the plaintiff has exhausted [his case], and the defendant, being asked, "Speak on this matter," does not speak—even though he is questioned repeatedly—if he does not respond because he lacks a valid answer, or because he speaks a false answer, thinking, "By this very fact my defeat occurs; but if I remain silent, there would be doubt regarding my defeat," then he too is defeated. And the author will state the limitation of time in this regard: "If he should not speak within three fortnights" (MDh 8.58). For one who is immediately summoned, a delay of time is appropriate due to the lack of understanding of the plaintiff's case and the failure to comprehend the reply. In this context, the completion of the three fortnights refers to one who speaks only slightly over five, ten, or twelve days, but not to one who remains entirely silent for such a duration. Furthermore, as for the period exceeding this—namely, "Even if the case is settled, one may wait for a year in case of a lack of presence of mind" (GDh 13.28)—it is not proper to respect that rule; for if a lack of presence of mind (*apratibhā*) is the reason for waiting, why would it be a non-reason if it were to occur after a year? Nor is there any rule established by any means that presence of mind arises for one lacking it after exactly one year. Therefore, only so many days of indulgence are appropriate as are required to determine the meaning of the plaintiff's case and for the reply to occur. Moreover, since this much time suffices even for a person of dull intellect, no further time should be allowed.

However, it is appropriate for the plaintiff (*pūrvapākṣika*) to establish his own case on that very day; for he has reached a certainty, thinking, "This person owes this to me," or "This person has done me this injury. He acts according to his own will and merely informs him of his own position; thus, how could his own interest remain unsettled? But the defendant (*uttarapākṣika*), being unaware of the connection and being brought before the king’s officers at that very moment, how indeed could he determine his own or the opposing side? For the investigation of both sides falls upon him at that very time; otherwise, one does not become a defendant. Therefore, regarding the matter to be proven, the conclusion of the plaintiff's case occurs on that day, or there is the gain of two days. Both of these positions are supported by other Smṛtis. For it says:
"The plaintiff should always establish his strength with firm certainty;
he should refine his own position for ten or twelve days.
Likewise, there is this other [rule]: "Then the claimant shall immediately have the proof of the matter asserted written down" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.7).

As for the examination of the year, that is not authoritative because its source is impossible; for it cannot be said that this Smṛti on legal procedure has the Veda as its source—unlike the Aṣṭakā rites and others—because its subject matter is not of the nature of an action (kārya). Furthermore, it has been established that such a source is impossible when the matter falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
This [rule] regarding the neglect of the three sides is not universal; as it is said:
"In cases of violence, theft, verbal assault, false accusation regarding cattle, and in matters concerning women..."
"One should initiate a lawsuit immediately; in other cases, the time is said to depend on one's own will. (YDh 2.12)

For if a case of violence (*sāhasa*) and the like were neglected for a long time, one might instead gratify the adversary. Therefore, a lawsuit is prescribed to be settled immediately. Furthermore, in this case, the aforementioned grounds for non-prosecution—such as loss of memory (*asmṛti*) and so forth—cannot possibly apply. This is because the cause of violence and the like must be reported to the king at that very moment; for there is an intense sense of urgency (*saṃvega*) in such matters. Moreover, if there is neglect due to the theft of clothing and other items, suspicion of complicity (*rāga-śaṅkā*) arises. Witnesses may also happen to be present there by chance; yet, having gone to another country, they cannot be identified by their names, castes, and so forth. Consequently, there is an absence of natural means of proof (*svābhāvika-pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, in matters such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*), the parties sometimes reach a mutual settlement; in such cases, there is no intervention by the king. Moreover, when a matter is generally settled, the recollection of how much was given is of little use at that time. However, one who commits an act of violence (*sāhasakārī*) must necessarily be punished by the king, even if he attempts to settle with the other party. Therefore, it is established that in cases such as debts, time may be allowed to elapse, whereas in cases of violence and the like, action must be immediate. As it has been said: "Because of the complexity of legal disputes and because of the incapacity of memory, one may allow time to pass in cases such as debts, if one desires to ascertain the truth. (NSm Mā 1.38)

When the plaintiff's case is confused, it cannot be grasped due to its complexity. Even if a case is unconfused, though its sequence may have been lost, it cannot be remembered in its entirety by everyone at the time of the response because of its magnitude; such is the meaning of the other Smṛti text. And it has been said: "He shall not fail to demonstrate [his case]. Having pointed out the matter to be proven, he does not prove it because of the absence of proof, or because the proof exists for the contrary side. Nor shall he know what comes before and after; this has already been stated. Therefore, he loses on account of the matter—that is, the subject of the legal dispute—and becomes defeated; such is the meaning. (8.56)
Having said, "There are witnesses who know [the facts] regarding me," if one who has been told to point them out does not do so,
the judge, by these reasons, shall declare him to be devoid of merit.

When one says, "I have witnesses who know [the facts]," and upon being told, "Let them speak," he remains silent—failing to identify them by their country, name, caste, or distinguishing attributes—then, for each of these previously stated reasons, he is declared here as "deficient" and fallen from the legal proceeding. The judge (*dharmastha*), presiding over the court of justice (*dharmādhikaraṇa*), should pronounce with certainty: "This man is defeated. Just as defeat occurs through the non-occurrence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that subverts the opposing side, so too does it occur due to the absence of a proof for one's own position. Furthermore, the ascertainment of non-existence [of such proof] arises from its failure to be presented again and again on the appropriate occasion, and from the non-presentation of any other supporting reason.

The word *jñātā* ends in the suffix *tṛn*. In that context, it is appropriate for it to be construed with the accusative ending in *idam*, because of the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *khalartha-tṛnām* (Pāṇini 2.3.69). The reading *hīnam tam* has the accusative ending. The particle *iti* should be understood as having the sense of "in this manner. One should point out that [the object] is deficient in these aforementioned ways and others of this kind. However, when there is a reference to the meaning of the entire sentence (*vākyārtha*), then the reading is *hīno 'sau*; since the meaning of the sentence functions as the object, there is no occurrence of the accusative case.

These are the grounds for defeat (*parājaya-hetu*). However, they are not fallible (*vyabhicārin*) in the same way that facial expressions, gestures, and so forth might be. For when someone does not present themselves at the time of repeated deliberation, or, though present, does not provide an answer, it becomes certain in that case: "He possesses no ground for victory. Moreover, if the king were never to defeat one who consistently fails to offer an answer, then the established order of the legal process would collapse. As for the failure to comprehend the sequence of the argument (*paurvāparya-anavabodha*), this should be understood as being like [the inference from] gestures and the like. When a person is always eloquent, bold, and resourceful, his changing gestures and so forth serve as corroborative evidence—standing in the place of a perceived mark (*liṅga-darśana*)—even when the ground for defeat has not yet been determined by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (8.57)
If the plaintiff does not speak, he should be bound and punished according to the law; if he does not speak within three fortnights regarding the matter of justice, he is defeated. (8.58)

If the plaintiff (*abhiyoktṛ*), being the claimant, does not state the subject matter of the legal dispute (*vyavahārapada*) after having summoned some person to the presence of the king, then he should be bound and punished for his lack of purpose. Regarding the punishment, imprisonment, and the measure of the fine, these should be determined by considering the merits of the defendant, the summoning [of witnesses], and the loss [sustained]. Therefore, the claimant must litigate on that very day. As for the meaning "if the defendant does not speak within three fortnights" (*tripakṣāt*): in that case, he is neither to be punished nor imprisoned. Rather, if he provides a reply within this time, he is indeed not defeated. "In accordance with *dharma*" means that this defeat is according to the law alone, not through trickery (*chala*). The form *tripakṣāt* (from three fortnights) should be understood as belonging to the group beginning with *pātra*; hence, there is no elision of the final vowel (*ikāra*). The true meaning of this verse has already been explained by us previously. (8.58)
Whatever amount of wealth one may conceal, or whatever amount one may falsely state, both of those ignorant of the law shall be made by the king to pay a fine double that amount. (8.59)

When it is determined by other means of proof that five thousand [paṇas] were given, yet ten are recorded in the document (*lekhyādi*)—having determined that another means of proof exists in the form of the year—one observes this: he who proceeds everywhere relying solely on the authority of the document is a litigant engaged in fraud (*chalavyavahārī*) and shall be fined double. But for one whose deviation from the truth is suspected even due to forgetfulness, the fine is ten percent. The same applies to the other party. It is not the case that there is a ten-percent fine for denying the whole and a double fine for denying a part; rather, those two who act otherwise out of deceit are to be fined double. For those who act out of forgetfulness or poverty, the fine is higher. To whatever extent the debtor (*adhamarṇa*) denies—that is, conceals—the amount, and to whatever extent the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) states a false—that is, a contrary—amount of wealth, to that same extent both the creditor and the debtor are ignorant of the law (*adharmajñau*). The fine is double. The word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the denied wealth; the fine (*dama*) or punishment is double that which was denied. And because of the mention of "ignorant of the law," it is stated that this penalty applies specifically to cases of proven fraud. (8.59)

But one who, having been questioned by a seeker of wealth and remaining steadfast, denies [the debt], must be proven [guilty] by at least three witnesses in the presence of the king and Brahmins. (8.60)

One who has reached the stage of being summoned, accused, and for whom a surety has been taken, is questioned by the judge or others in the presence of the king: "Do you owe this person [the debt], or not? Being thus questioned, he denies it—that is, he conceals it. By one seeking wealth—desiring to recover his own previously lent property—he who is in dispute must be made to prove it through witnesses; that is, he must be made to establish his case. "By at least three" (*tryavaraiḥ*): those of whom three are the minimum are "at least three. The word *avara* expresses the limit of decrease. If they are absolutely fewer, then there should be three; otherwise, more than three. "In the presence of the king and the Brahmins," and so forth.

But surely, for those very persons by whom the legal proceeding has been initiated, the interrogation of witnesses is required to take place in their very presence; what is the purpose of this requirement that it be done "in the presence of the king and Brāhmaṇas"?

It is not so, because the interrogation of witnesses can also be accomplished by sending a person of authority [to them]. Therefore, the repetition of the rule is to ensure that they must be questioned directly. (8.60)
I shall now fully describe the kind of witnesses who should be appointed by wealthy men in legal proceedings, and how the truth must be spoken by them. (8.61)

This verse introduces the characteristics of witnesses: I shall describe, as will be stated hereafter, the kind of witnesses—of what caste and endowed with what qualities—who should be employed by creditors (dhanins) in legal proceedings involving the lending of money and similar matters; and I shall also explain the manner in which truth (*ṛtam*) or reality (*satyam*) must be spoken by those good men when questioned, beginning with the rule that it should be done in the forenoon and so forth. (8.61)

Householders who have sons, who are native-born, and who belong to the kṣatriya, vaiśya, or śūdra castes, being summoned by the plaintiff, are worthy of serving as witnesses; no others whatsoever are so, except in times of emergency. (8.62)

Householders are those who have taken a wife; the word "house" (*gṛha*) refers here to a wife. For they do not practice deceit out of fear of being disgraced by their own wives. Some people, even though they are indifferent toward themselves, speak falsehoods with the thought: "We shall protect ourselves by traveling to another land," or "We shall remain hidden right here somewhere," or "We shall acquire wealth or friends. Householders, however, because of their concern for their family, think: "Where would we not protect ourselves? and thus, having set aside [self-interest], they do not act otherwise due to their regard for their family and their fear of royal punishment.

"Those who have sons": they are called "those who have sons" because of their affection for their children. Furthermore, one who has neither son nor wife may, at the time of questioning witnesses, even if he is of good conduct, sometimes not be present; for he does not reside permanently in a single place. In this same way, the *maula* witnesses are also to be explained. *Maulāḥ* are those from the countryside (*jānapada*) who are natives of that region. For, out of fear of sin, they do not speak falsely among their own kin and relatives. *Mūla* means foundation or established status; those who possess this are *maula*. This is an explanation of the meaning of the term. However, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) should be understood as expressing the abstract state (*bhāvārtha*). For it is not contradictory to say that one who is born in a certain place also possesses that place.

The *kṣatriya*, *vaiśya*, and *śūdra* castes [are eligible], but not the *brāhmaṇa*. For for him, both study and teaching are prescribed at all times, or else the daily *agnihotra* sacrifice must be performed. In that case, lest there be an obstruction to his religious duties (*dharma*) while the king is far away, he is not appointed by way of being a duty. However, one who has understood the matter spontaneously is the most principal witness in a serious legal proceeding when other witnesses are absent. Accordingly, there will be an interrogation of witnesses such as: "One should ask the *brāhmaṇa*: 'Speak! (MDh 8.88). The word *yoni* (source/birth) is connected with each [of the preceding terms]. One whose source—meaning birth or cause—is the *kṣatra* is a *kṣatrayoni*; the meaning is "one belonging to the *kṣatriya* caste. Alternatively, the compound is also explained by the analysis of the rule regarding the fifth case (*pañcamī-yogavibhāga*), namely: "one whose source—meaning birth—is from the *kṣatra*. When they are pointed out by the plaintiff as "these are my witnesses," then they become fit for the function of witnessing; however, those who come of their own accord to give testimony are not [formal] witnesses.

"In the absence of an emergency. Some say that an "emergency" means the absence of other witnesses; however, that is incorrect. The reason for not being a witness is the tendency toward contradiction; this does not disappear simply because there are no other witnesses to corroborate him. We do not mean to say that those whose status as witnesses is prohibited—such as those who have reasons for telling lies, like having a financial interest in the case—are permitted in this situation. Rather, this is an exception granted for those, such as Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), for whom there would be a conflict with dharma if they were summoned, provided that no other witnesses exist who have personally experienced the matter; it is not, however, for those who are habitually untruthful. (8.62)
Trustworthy persons from all castes should be made witnesses in legal matters, provided they are knowers of all dharmas and free from greed; however, one should avoid those who are the opposite.

The *āptas* (trustworthy persons) are those who are non-deceptive, who speak of things exactly as they have perceived them, and whose capacity for deception the world does not suspect; they are renowned as being devoted to the practice of *dharma*. They are knowers of all *dharma*—that is, they know every *dharma*, whether based on the Vedas (*śrauta*), the Smṛtis (*smārta*), or established by custom (*ācāra-nirūḍha*)—leaving nothing out, such as that "in this case hell is the fruit" or "in this case heaven is the fruit. For they fear speaking untruth, seeing hell [awaiting them]. They are free from greed and noble-minded, not regarding even a small amount of wealth as much. Each of these qualifications applies to every individual witness, because they function as qualities in the act of witnessing, and in the case of a quality, their collective presence is intended. "In all castes" (*sarveṣu varṇeṣu*) means that in all legal matters (*sarvakāryeṣu*), there is no restriction based on caste; this is what is being stated. As for the mention of caste regulations, we shall explain that further below. This is what is meant: in all legal matters, such as the non-payment of debts (*ṛṇādāna*) and so forth, all castes may be made witnesses as far as possible, provided they possess the aforementioned characteristics. However, one should avoid those who are the opposite. Although there is no possibility of the opposite occurring once specific [virtuous] persons have been mentioned, this is nevertheless an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) common in worldly usage. Generally, worldly people establish one thing and then prohibit its opposite. Thus people say: "Action disciplines a person of substance, not one lacking substance. Furthermore, non-deceptiveness is the primary characteristic of a witness here, and that cannot be determined through a positive injunction, but rather through the absence of the causes of deception. For non-deceptiveness is not perceptible to the senses; it consists of speaking according to the facts. And in the case of an object perceivable only by hearing, how can there be a perceptual certainty of the facts? If it were perceptible, there would be no need to seek the testimony of a witness at all. Nor is it possible in every case where an object is beyond the senses and known only through words to have corroboration by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, since those factors which are commonly seen to cause false speech are absent, non-deceptiveness is inferred through the certainty of that absence. Hence, this introductory statement—"but one should avoid those who are the opposite"—is intended to demonstrate that. (8.63)

Those who have financial interests, those who are not trustworthy, those who are allies, or those who are enemies; those whose faults are known, those afflicted by disease, or those who are corrupt—none of these should be appointed as attendants. (8.64)

These are enumerated as being capable of acting as instruments for false testimony. Among them, those connected by a financial interest are the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) and the debtor (*adhamarṇa*), and so forth. For when a creditor is defeated by the words of a debtor, he may, at that very moment, overcome by a fit of rage, obstruct the debtor from paying the wealth. Consequently, the debtor, conforming to the mind of the creditor who has the wealth at hand, is able to speak in accordance with his interests; therefore, he is not a witness. The creditor, too, is not a witness, for even though the debtor is penniless, he might—driven by the thought that "once I have won the lawsuit and obtained the wealth, this man will pay me back"—sometimes speak in favor of the debtor's side. Thus, he also is not a witness.

Alternatively, "artha" means purpose or motive. One who has some purpose to be accomplished by the two litigants through the witness, or by whom those two have a purpose to be accomplished, is not a witness because he possesses even a trace of self-interest. Or, one who shares the same result as the matter involved in the legal proceeding—those related to the case in such ways are excluded.

"Trusted persons" (āpta) are paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others who, by virtue of being friends or relatives, are intimately involved in one's affairs. "Helpers" (sahāya) are sureties and the like. "Enemies" (vairin) are well known. "Those of proven fault" (dṛṣṭadoṣa) are those who have given false testimony elsewhere, or who have practiced other prohibited acts. "Afflicted by disease" (vyādhyārta) means tormented by illness; the inclusion of the word "afflicted" (ārta) implies that those with merely slight ailments are not meant, for in one who is truly tormented, anger, forgetfulness, and so forth may lead to false testimony. "Corrupted" (dūṣita) refers to those who have committed mortal sins (pātakin) or those habitually practicing minor offenses (upapātaka). However, the mention of "those of proven fault" is intended to include even those very individuals who have already been punished, for they are no longer considered corrupted at present since their discipline has been enforced by kings through the imposition of punishment. (8.64)
A king shall not be made a witness, nor artisans or actors;
nor a Vedic scholar, nor one dwelling in a religious order, nor one who has renounced all worldly attachments. (8.65)

When a litigant says, "You shall be my witness," the king must not be requested to serve as a witness at the time of the disbursement of wealth or other matters. For if he were to give testimony, people might suspect him of partiality; or, because of his sovereign power, if he were to testify for one side, the case would be ruined. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to question him according to the rules governing witnesses. Moreover, even if a resident of that region might corroborate [the facts] through documents and the like, he might still fail to fulfill all the duties of a witness; thus, there is a prohibition against appointing the king residing in that region as a witness.

Artisans and others live by association out of fear that their own work might be obstructed. It is the nature of country folk that even when they have decided for themselves, "We shall live," they become angry with witnesses and the like once they are defeated. Consequently, the universal social cohesion of artisans and others is destroyed. Furthermore, because of their inherent fickleness, they can even be made to waver from their livelihood; thus, they may come to take sides.

However, regarding the status of a *śrotriya* as a witness, the obligation to testify is prohibited for him, just as it is for a king; this is not, however, due to a lack of trustworthiness. For being a *śrotriya* does not undermine credibility; on the contrary, it produces it especially. Indeed, being a *śrotriya* has never been observed to be a cause of contradiction. The same applies to subsequent cases as well.

Artisans are those who live by their crafts, such as cooks, blacksmiths, and the like. Actors include dancers, singers, and so forth. A *śrotriya* is one who recites the Vedas; here, however, one who is devoted to Vedic study is intended. Alternatively, the term *śrotriya* serves to indicate the performance of ritual duties (*karmānuṣṭhāna*); thus, there is a prohibition against one devoted to such performance because it would conflict with [the practice of yoga]. A *liṅgastha* is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*). Those who bear the marks of wandering mendicants or heretics are already excluded because they follow false scriptures. Householders who have renounced attachments are those who have renounced the Vedas; "attachment" refers either to the enjoyment of sense objects through habituation or to the undertaking of actions for visible worldly ends. (8.65)

Neither one who is dependent on another, nor one who is censurable, nor a thief, nor one who performs forbidden acts; neither an elderly man, nor a child, nor one alone, nor an outcaste, nor one with impaired faculties. (8.66)

The word *adhyadhīna* (dependent) is used by convention (*rūḍhi*) for those who are entirely dependent, such as a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*). Others, however, read it as *adhyādhīna* because the phonetic combination is similar; *adhyādhīna* means one made a pledge (*bandhakīkṛta*). A *vaktavya* (one to be instructed) refers to a pupil, a son, and so forth, because they are dependent on their teacher. Alternatively, it may refer to one whose body is deformed by leprosy or other diseases. A *dasyu* is a hired servant (*bhṛtidāsa*), a wage-earner (*vaitanika*); he is so defined in the *Nirukta* because "he brings near (*upādāsayati*)" his tasks. Since he is paid by the day, he does not have absolute dependence; thus, he is mentioned separately. If such persons were to live by performing work [for others], there would be a loss of their livelihood, and because of their low status, they might be untrustworthy due to the possibility of greed and other vices. As for a thief, since he is mentioned by a different term, he is not included under the category of *dasyu*. Or, a *dasyu* is one with a hard heart, one of cruel conduct. A *vikarmakṛt* (one who performs forbidden acts) is one who performs work contrary to the scriptures, such as a Brāhmaṇa following the occupation of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, and so forth. An *old man* (*vṛddha*) is one who, due to the decline of age, lacks memory. A *child* (*śiśu*) is a minor who has not attained legal capacity. Regarding the rule that at least three must be present: since one person is not obtained by the requirement of "at least three," this prohibition is intended to permit two in certain circumstances, just as in the case of a document written with three hands (where only two are actually needed). Even though a third scribe is not present there, someone might suspect that the mere act of writing does not constitute being a witness; [the rule clarifies this]. An *outcaste* (*anta*) is a Barbarian (*barbara*), a Caṇḍāla, and so forth, outside of one's own group. This is a prohibition of those who, by birth from a Śūdra womb, would otherwise be eligible. One with impaired senses (*vikalendriya*) includes the blind, the deaf, and so forth, whose perception is defective due to physical affliction. (8.66)
Neither one who is distressed, nor intoxicated, nor insane; neither one oppressed by hunger or thirst, nor afflicted by fatigue, nor tormented by desire, nor angry, nor even a thief. (8.67)

"Afflicted" (ārta) means one who has suffered the loss of relatives, wealth, and so forth. "Intoxicated" (matta) means one who is drunk from the intoxication of liquor. "Seized by epilepsy" (apasmāragṛhīta) means one who is insane or possessed by a *piśāca*. "Oppressed by hunger and thirst" (kṣuttṛṣṇopapīḍita) means one who is distressed by hunger and thirst. "Fatigue" (*śrama*) is that which arises from excessive physical exertion, such as traveling long distances or fighting; one afflicted by it is "pained" (*ārta*). "Lust" (*kāma*) is the desire for union with women; one afflicted by it is so because of the mental agitation caused by both separation and intense union, as well as the apprehension regarding the means to achieve them. "Angry" (*kruddha*) refers to one whose anger is directed toward many others; for since his mind is pervaded by anger, he neither experiences [the object] nor remembers what has been experienced. A "thief" (*taskara*) is a robber (*caura*); although he is already included among those who perform forbidden acts (*vikarmakṛt*), he is mentioned separately according to the maxim of "cattle and oxen" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). (8.67)
Women shall give testimony for women; twice-born men of similar status for twice-born men; virtuous Śūdras for Śūdras; and those of low birth for those of the lowest castes. (8.68)

Where the two parties—the plaintiff and the defendant—are both men, there women do not serve as witnesses. However, where a man has a legal matter with a woman, or where there is a minor mutual dispute among women themselves, in those cases women certainly may be witnesses. Nor is this a fixed rule that women must give testimony only for women and never for men; rather, women are permitted as witnesses only in certain cases involving male subjects, because the reason "due to their instability" (MDh 8.77) is cited. There are indeed some women who, like female exponents of the Veda (*brahmavādinī*), are speakers of truth and possess steady intellects.

"Among the twice-born (*dvija*), those who are similar [to the litigant] are the twice-born witnesses. A twice-born witness who is of superior authority, even if he provides testimony that appears inconsistent and whose reliability is doubted, does not become one whose word is untrustworthy; for such a person must be regarded as being of authoritative status himself, since he is indeed similar to him. For among those who are similar, staying in the same locality and mutual knowledge of each other's affairs are considered possible. But for another [who is dissimilar], proximity to that place must be achieved through effort. However, in the case of two similar persons, this is established by natural fitness (*aucitya*). Likewise, for an inferior person, one of inferior quality may also be accepted from among those who are similar; but one of superior quality should not be excluded. Similarity may exist through caste, craft and the like, or through qualities, actions such as Vedic study, or through common character. And this [rule] is to be observed in matters that are not of great importance; for trustworthiness is not determined among those of inferior qualities."

And for the lowest castes, such as the Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas, there are likewise those of the lowest birth (*antyayoni*). "Lowest" (*antya*) means "existing at the end. The analysis of the compound is: "those whose *yoni*—that is, their cause of origin—is that [lowest]. This is merely an illustration; for even those not mentioned here, such as merchants, artisans, and bards, who are equal in terms of caste, craft, character, and so forth, [are to be married among equals], because the reason [for this rule] is the same. (8.68)
But whoever, being an eyewitness, should give testimony for litigants in a private house, in a forest, or even in a matter involving the loss of life; 8.69.

In cases where an act occurs within the interior of a house—such as verbal or physical assault, adultery, theft, or violence—which has arisen unexpectedly, or where such an act occurs in the forest; or when a person is being physically harmed by bandits or others at that very moment and seized from somewhere; or when someone has been appointed as a surety for the sake of wealth, yet witnesses cannot be found or do not wait for that duration of time; or when a matter is discussed in private and they take the wealth without public disclosure—in such circumstances, anyone who is an eyewitness (*anubhāvī*) should be accepted as a witness. An *anubhāvī* is one who has directly perceived [the event]. By the phrase "anyone whatsoever," there is no restriction regarding caste; he says this because at such a time, a similar person may not be available.

The phrase "within the house" (*antarveśmani*) is intended to indicate a place where people are sparse; by this, even empty temples and the like, which are sparsely populated, are included. Likewise, the mention of the forest (*araṇya*) is for the purpose of illustrating this very same point.

Others, however, explain the phrase "and also upon the death of the body" differently: when the body that serves as the instrument for action perishes, whoever is a witness—regarding an action that, once commenced, lapses and becomes impossible to perform at a later time—in that case there is no restriction based on caste, gender, age, similarity, or relationship among the witnesses. He demonstrates this very point with the following verse (8.69).
In the absence of a woman, the duty may be performed by a child, an elderly person, a disciple, a relative, or even a slave or a hired servant. (8.70)

The change of gender is stated by the word "striyā" (by a woman). The change of age is indicated by "by a child or an old man. The phrase beginning with "by a pupil" (*śiṣyeṇa*) constitutes a counter-exception regarding related persons. This is merely an illustration for the purpose of showing that such rules may have exceptions; therefore, even when there is similarity of caste, they are not strictly adhered to. However, friends, enemies, those who have seen faults [in lying], and others are not permitted [to testify]. Those whose capacity to cause the utterance of untruth has been observed, but which is neither pervasive nor universal, are not counter-exceptioned. But those whose [capacity] is very pervasive, yet occurs only in certain cases due to an excellence of virtue—if it should deviate from this rule, then in those specific instances, they are witnesses. And it has been said:
"One might obtain a thousand [pieces of gold] neither from a friend nor from an enemy, nor even through a connection of wealth; yet a man should never practice untruth."

In the absence of other witnesses, even a woman may serve as a witness. What [is required]? The word "witnessing" (*sākṣyam*) is supplied from the preceding verse. The mention of "by a pupil" (*śiṣyeṇa*) is intended to demonstrate a relationship based on the *mukha* (mouth) and *sruva* (ladle)—that is, the teacher-pupil bond. The mention of "by a kinsman" (*bandhunā*) is an exception to the rule regarding those who are not to be excluded due to innate or matrimonial kinship; even though such a person is a relative, one who is not too closely related is included. Therefore, a brother-in-law, a maternal uncle, a brother-in-law by marriage, and others are not witnesses, for the word "kinsman" (*bandhu*) is conventionally used in that sense. By the mention of "by a slave" (*dāsena*), the master-servant relationship is indicated. However, the master, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), and the officiating priest (*yājaka*) are not witnesses in any circumstance. A "slave" (*dāsa*) here refers to a slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*). A "hired servant" (*bhṛtaka*) is one who works for wages (*vaitanika*).

But surely, children and others have been excluded from being witnesses due to their incapacity. For they are not able to ascertain testimony because of the instability of their intellect and defects such as immaturity; thus, its restoration in times of distress is improper, for capacity does not manifest in this person during a time of distress. It would be like someone saying, "New rice should not be cooked; however, it should be cooked when there is fire. This is not a fault; it is precisely for this purpose that the following verse is commenced. (8.70)
One should recognize that the speech of children, the elderly, and the sick, when they testify falsely, as well as that of those with agitated minds, is unstable. (8.71)

This is its meaning: here, children and others whose minds are entirely untrained, bound by delusion, or confused are not intended, for [if they were], the matter taught would be something to be undertaken [by them]. Rather, it is permitted for those who are capable of discerning [the truth] but whose minds are not overly steady; their speech must be examined by means of inference. If they speak coherently, do not falter, and are not associated with any suspected defect, then they are authoritative. Regarding this, he says: "One should recognize the speech of those speaking falsely as unstable. This is what is meant: one should determine falsity by the instability of speech. In that context, instability of speech consists of the mutual incoherence of words and the indistinctness or incompleteness of syllables. And this is intended as an illustration of the condition of children and the like. Furthermore, those who—due to age or disease—have reached such a state that they utter something else when intending to say another thing, and even that indistinctly, are not witnesses. This cause of non-witnesshood is perceptible to the senses. But other [grounds], common to passion, hatred, greed for wealth, and so forth, are to be examined through inference. And that has already been stated: "Those whose minds are arrogant, who are by nature agitated, and whose intellects are lacking in firmness... (8.71).
In all cases of violence, theft, and adultery, as well as in verbal and physical assault, one should not examine the witnesses too closely. (8.72)

*Sa-ha* means force; that which is done by relying upon that is *sāhasa* (an act of violence). An improper act committed through the king’s favor, by virtue of having a large following, by the strength of one's own body, or by relying on a powerful patron—that is *sāhasa*, such as [the examples at] 8.276: tearing clothes, setting fire [to property], cutting hair, and so forth. The rest is well known. In this case, witnesses are not to be examined. The examination consisting of the criteria such as "householders who have sons" (MDh 8.62) and so forth is prohibited here. However, that which is suspected of being a cause for deviation—consisting of passion, hatred, greed for wealth, and so forth—must certainly be investigated. For it has been stated that this Smṛti rule has its basis in visible reality. 8.72.

In the event of a conflict between witnesses, O King, the ruler should accept the majority; but when the numbers are equal, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and when there is a conflict even among those possessed of virtue, he should accept the best of the twice-born.

In cases where there is a dispute regarding a plot of land or the like, and witnesses have been cited by both parties as proof of possession—where some claimants assert possession while others, the defendants, deny it—the testimony of the majority should be accepted. However, if they are equal in number, those who are superior in qualities (guṇa)—meaning those possessing many qualities—or those endowed with a single quality that is preeminent and beneficial to the perceived human purpose, should be preferred. If there is a difference among those of equal merit, caste (jāti) must be taken into account. In the event of total equality, an oath (śapatha) or something else equivalent to it should be administered.
One should accept the majority; one should take the word of the many as authoritative. Duality is the statement of mutually contradictory meanings. 8.73
Testimony is established through seeing in person and likewise through hearing;
in that regard, a witness who speaks the truth does not fall away from dharma and artha. (8.74)

But has this not already been stated by the verse, "Whoever, however, is an eyewitness... (MDh 8.69)? How can a possibility of alternative proof be suspected, such that it must be said here that the establishment of witness-hood occurs through seeing and hearing?

To this it is replied: A witness must be appointed by one who intends to litigate, saying, "You shall be my witness. In that case, one who has not been so addressed would not otherwise qualify. It is for this purpose that the following is stated: even if one who was present there is some way a direct experiencer and is not told, "You ought to remember this matter between us two," he nonetheless becomes a witness, because of his direct seeing (*samakṣadarśana*)—that is, through direct experience or hearing. The word *samakṣa* (in the presence of) must be supplied [to both terms]. When something is heard from someone by one person, and then heard by another from him, that is hearsay; one who hears it through such a chain is not a witness. For instance, when it comes to public rumor—"This man has committed this wrongful act" or "He owes this much to him"—it is based on worldly renown rather than on formal proof. In this context, "direct seeing" means direct experience regarding the subject matter; [this includes] what is directly seen with the operation of the eyes, such as the lending of money, the infliction of punishment, or physical assault; likewise, "hearing" refers to the hearing of words regarding matters such as verbal abuse, or "I have received this from him," and so forth. Although the root *dṛś* (to see) denotes perception in general, nevertheless, for the sake of following the meter, auditory cognition (*śrotrajñāna*) is mentioned separately as "hearing" (*śravaṇa*). This much is intended here: he by whom something has been experienced through a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is a witness. The inclusion of the word *samakṣa* is for the purpose of indicating any means of valid knowledge in general. Therefore, even what is experienced through inference and so forth is indeed "experienced. Thus, what is heard from authoritative tradition (*āptāgama*), though not perceptible, is a valid means of knowledge. The latter half of the verse, however, is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), since speaking the truth has already been enjoined, and the loss of merit and wealth for a speaker of untruth is already understood through other means of knowledge. (8.74)
A witness who gives testimony in an assembly of noble men concerning anything other than what was seen or heard goes headlong to hell after death and is excluded from heaven. (8.75)

This [verse] is intended to show the consequences for witnesses who speak untruth. It has been stated that the word *dṛṣṭa-śruta* (seen and heard) is a synonym for *upalabdhi* (perceived). Therefore, anything other than that is *anupalabdha* (unperceived).
