If he speaks of such [a thing], then, O noble ones, members of the assembly, you who act rightly—in their presence, in the court—he goes with his face cast down, downward, to hell, a place of torment; having died, he falls away from heaven. Even the merit earned by him through rites for ascending to heaven is obstructed by the gravity of the sin of false testimony. However, there is no destruction of the merit for heaven by another sin, because actions yield their own specific fruits, except in cases of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). (8.75)
Even where one might see or hear something unintentionally, one should speak of it there exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard. (8.76)

But was it not already stated under the rule "because of seeing in person" (MDh 8.74) that there is testimony even for one who has experienced [the event] in any way whatsoever, even if not formally appointed? In that case, what is the purpose of this [rule], "even where one is not recorded," or what is the distinction?

It is said: Witnesshood is appropriate for one who has been entered upon a document due to a specific transaction and so forth, but not for one who has not been so entered. For if both were witnesses, it would result in the document's entry being rendered useless. Therefore, to dispel this doubt, the following is stated. The previous verse [8.54] refers to cases where witnesses are not recorded; this verse, however, refers to cases where there is a document accompanied by witnesses. "Unrecorded" means even one who has not been entered upon the document. The terms "seeing" and "hearing" have already been explained. The remainder is easily understood. (8.76)

A single person may be a witness even if they are greedy, but many women, even if they are pure, cannot be; for the intellect of women is unstable, and others who are tainted by faults [should likewise not be witnesses]. (8.77)

Furthermore, the prohibition of a single witness is for the purpose of an exception (*pratiprasava*) in the case of one who is free from greed and other such defects. Therefore, even a single witness becomes admissible if he is determined to be truthful. However, women—whether few or many—are never fit to be witnesses, even if they are pure; that is to say, even if they possess virtuous qualities. The reason for this is: "Because of the instability of the female intellect. It is the very nature of women that their intellect is fickle. As for virtues, even if acquired through effort, they may vanish due to negligence, laziness, and so forth; thus, natural instability remains constant. Just as in the case of a person suffering from a chronic illness, even if the digestive fire is stabilized by means of ghee and other remedies, the innate condition of the illness recurs upon even the slightest lapse in care. For this reason, there can be no reliance on them, even when they possess virtues, due to this apprehension. As for the rule, "In the absence [of others], it may be done even by a woman" (MDh 8.70), that refers to cases where they are questioned at that very moment, and where there is no suspicion that their minds have been swayed by anyone. But where there is an interval of time, they might perhaps be won over by the losing party; therefore, in such cases, women are never to be witnesses.

"And others who are beset by defects (*doṣaiḥ*). This means those men other than women who are beset—that is, overcome—by defects such as diseases and the like; the sense is that they possess an abundance of defects. What, then, are these so-called "defects"? It has been said: "Passion and the rest, which are prohibited by the scriptures and whose nature as causes for suspected infidelity [is established]. Although the defects have already been mentioned by their own specific names, this [present mention] is not redundant for the purpose of including those not previously mentioned. For authors everywhere accept the practice of stating both the general and the particular.

Others, however, by eliding the vowel *a* [in the compound], explain it thus: "Even one who is not greedy (*alubdha*) is not a witness, much less one who is greedy. In this way, the testimony of two witnesses is permitted.

Furthermore, the long vowel *ī* in the word *śucya* is difficult to justify, because of the rule "after a word denoting a quality ending in *u*, the feminine suffix *ūṅ* is applied" (Pāṇini 4.1.44). Some, however, support its validity by appealing to the rule "from a word ending in the *ik*-pratyaya" (Pāṇini 4.1.45). 8.77.
Whatever they might say by their very nature is to be accepted as conventional;
therefore, whatever else they might speak for the sake of dharma is meaningless. 8.78

Whatever witnesses state naturally in accordance with the facts of the case is to be accepted. However, if they speak for the sake of dharma with a mind that has deviated from the truth due to a sense of righteousness, that is useless and not to be accepted; this is the meaning. That which is a statement of a matter exactly as it was seen is [spoken] by nature. But that which is otherwise—done with the thought, "May there be no harm to this poor man because of my words"—is useless. For example, someone might report, "I was insulted by this man. Thereupon, the other party denies it. The witnesses say: "It is true he was insulted, but in jest, not out of anger. In that case, the witnesses' statement that "he was insulted" is to be accepted. However, the part "in jest" is not to be accepted, even though it was spoken, because it was not asked and was stated by the defendant without being questioned.

"Conventional" (*vyāvahārika*) means pertaining to common worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). "Purposeless" (*apagataprayojana*) means lacking meaning (*apārthaka*). Others explain: when those who are timid and so forth utter faltering words, one should not reject them on that account alone; rather, their true disposition must be discerned through inference—namely, whether they stumble due to timidity or because of a tendency toward untruthful speech. That, however, has been stated previously. Furthermore, one should not disregard the literal meaning of the words. (8.78)

When the witnesses have arrived within the assembly hall in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant, the judge shall examine them, consoling them with this procedure: "Speak the truth as you know it; speak the truth in this matter. For by speaking the truth in judicial proceedings, you shall attain both this world and the next. But by speaking falsehood when questioned in a court of law, you shall fall headlong into hell after death, experiencing the torments of Yama’s servants. The gods know not a man more contemptible than one who, having entered the court, speaks what is contrary to the facts. The gods, together with Indra and the Brahmins, know the man who, having entered the court, bears false witness. He who gives false testimony regarding small cattle, land, gold, silver, or grain—each of these [false witnesses] shall be punished with the penalty prescribed for theft. || 8.79 ||

*Sabhāyām antaḥ* means "within the assembly. This is a compound formed according to the *śauṇḍādi* group (cf. Pāṇini 2.1.40). Those who have gone to the place of legal proceedings (*vyavahāradeśa*) must be questioned in the presence of both the plaintiff and the defendant, according to the procedure to be described hereafter. He should do so while "consoling," that is, speaking without harshness. For if he speaks harshly, those who are afraid of the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) might not remain in their natural state and thus would not remember everything, since fear is a cause for the loss of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). The term *prāḍvivāka* is used by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) to denote the official appointed by the king to oversee legal proceedings, even though its etymological meaning ("one who asks and discriminates") could also apply to the king himself. Nevertheless, we see it used in distinction from him: "Whether it be a minister or a judge (*prāḍvivāka*) who should decide a case otherwise... (MDh 9.234). The word *prāṭ* is derived from the root *pracch* ("to ask") with the suffix *kvip*, according to the rule: "*kvib-vaci-pracchi-śri-dru-śru-pruvāṃ dīrgho 'saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca*" (the vowel is lengthened and there is no *samprasāraṇa* change). He is a *vivāka* because he "discriminates" (*vi-vic*) especially in matters of legal difficulty (*dharma-saṃkaṭa*). The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.3.113 (*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*). By Pāṇini 7.3.52 (*cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*), the *c* is changed to *k*, resulting in *vivāka*. Thus, one who is both a *prāṭ* and a *vivāka* is a *prāḍvivāka*. (8.79)
"Whatever you two know of each other's conduct regarding this matter, tell it all in truth; for your witness is required here. (8.80)

"Whatever you know regarding the mutual conduct or behavior of these two in this legal matter—whether witnessed publicly or in secret—declare and relate all of that truthfully and accurately. For your testimony is required here; your authority lies in this case. Truth and falsehood depend upon your words. By this they are encouraged. Although there is a general designation that "you are witnesses in this case," it should be understood by implication that the entirety of the matter must be heard, for those who have not heard the particulars are not capable of knowing the subject of the inquiry. (8.80)
By speaking the truth in his testimony, a witness attains irreproachable worlds; and in this world, he gains unsurpassed fame—this word is honored by Brahmā. (8.81)

From this point forward is the rule for the interrogation of witnesses concerning truthful speech. By speaking the truth, a witness attains blameless and irreproachable worlds characterized by heaven and the like, which serve as the cause for the enjoyment of desired fruits. Alternatively, the word *loka* may signify "birth"; the meaning is that he is born into an auspicious birth. And in this life, he obtains unsurpassed fame—that renown than which there is nothing higher or more excellent—and the people bestow upon him the praise of being a virtuous man. For this speech, Truth, is Sarasvatī, worshipped by Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures. (8.81)
Speaking untruth when testifying, one is bound tightly with the nooses of Varuṇa for a hundred future births, rendered helpless; therefore, one should speak the truth as a witness. (8.82)

By the previous [verse], which showed the visible and invisible results of good and evil, witnesses were encouraged to speak the truth. By this [verse], the arising of suffering from speaking falsely is shown; this is solely for the sake of truthful speech. *Sākṣya* is the duty of a witness. Therein, one who speaks untruth is bound and tormented by the nooses of Varuṇa, excessively (*bhṛśam*) and beyond measure. He is rendered helpless (*vivaśaḥ*), his independence lost even in all his movements, including those of speech and sight. For as many as a hundred births, the terrible nooses of Varuṇa—consisting of serpent-ropes or dropsy—persist. The injunction is that one should speak the truth in order to avoid this fault. In the word *ājātīḥ*, the prefix *āṅ* does not signify a limit or inclusion; if it did, there would have been a fifth case ending. Therefore, this prefix is meaningless, as in the case of *pralambate*. Furthermore, this is an accusative, and repetition (*āvṛtti*) is understood here: he revolves through a hundred births, seized by the belly. (8.82)
A witness is purified by truth; righteousness increases through truth.
Therefore, truth must indeed be spoken by witnesses among all social classes.
It is purified, it becomes clean; that is to say, it is liberated even from other sins. The rest has already been explained. || 8.83 ||
For the self alone is the witness of the self, and the self is likewise the refuge of the self.
Do not despise your own self, the supreme witness of men. (8.84)
This very point is made clear by the following verse. || 8.84 ||
"Evildoers indeed think, 'No one sees us';
yet the gods see them, as does their own inner self. (8.85)

The word *na* is displaced [in the verse]. Those who commit evil deeds, such as those who practice fraud and the like, think: "No one sees us. By the particle *iti*, it is shown that the object of the verb *man* (to think) is the meaning of the entire sentence. The meaning of the sentence is: "No one sees us. However, the gods—who will be described below—see them, as does their own inner self (*antarātman*). As it has been said: "For the self alone is the witness of the self" (MDh 8.84). Now, who indeed is this evildoer, and who else is his witness? For the self alone is the agent of good and evil deeds, and the inner person (*antarapuruṣa*) is the witness.

True. Having superimposed divinity upon that very [Self], the designation of it as both object and agent through differentiation is for the purpose of ceasing falsehood. You know the form of the deity; however, you are exhorted: "Do not commit evil for the sake of enjoying this internal, corporeal form which is your true nature, nor for the sake of this external, non-self, and insubstantial [form]. Therefore: "Do not despise your own Self, the unsurpassed witness of men" (MDh 8.84). For another witness exists only in this world, but this one gives testimony even for one who has died. Therefore, one must fear this [Self]. A liar might sometimes think: "Once I have attained another body, what will this witness do to me? That is not so: "The Self is likewise the refuge of the Self" (MDh 8.84). There is no other refuge apart from the Self; for there are not two selves belonging to a single person.
Others, however, think that there is a distinction: the Supreme Self is the witness, while the transmigrating selves are those to be enjoined. (8.85)
Who, then, are those gods who perceive one even when practicing evil in secret? To this he says:
"Heaven, earth, water, the heart, the moon, the sun, fire, Yama, and the wind;
night, the two twilights, and Dharma—these know the conduct of all embodied beings. (8.86)

By the word "heart" (hṛdaya), the subtle person (liṅgapuruṣa) residing in the heart is meant. Regarding heaven and the other [worlds], the capacity to see—which is consciousness—is superimposed upon these insentient things. However, in another philosophical system, the great elements are indeed sentient by virtue of being the very nature of deities. Thus it is described that the Earth approached Brahmā for the removal of her burden. Because they are all-pervading, there is nothing that is not within their range of perception; therefore, they know the conduct and character of all embodied beings, as well as every auspicious and inauspicious action pertaining to the body of the self. (8.86)

In the presence of the gods and Brahmins, the judge, being himself pure, should question the pure twice-born men regarding the truth in the forenoon, while they face either the north or the east. (8.87)

The gods, such as Durgā, Mārtaṇḍa, and others, are represented by images. [He should approach] those who are pure, having performed the prescribed rites of bathing, sipping water (ācamana), and so forth. The questioner himself should likewise be pure. The word "ṛtam" is used merely for the purpose of completing the verse. The rest is well known. 8.87.
One should ask a Brāhmaṇa, "Speak"; a king, "Speak the truth"; a Vaiśya, with [threats of] cattle, grain, and gold; and a Śūdra, with these [same] sins. (8.88)

But where does this third [instrumental case] come from in the phrase "by means of cows, seeds, and gold"? If it is argued that it is called an instrument because of its connection with the action expressed by the verb "if one should ask" (*yadi tāvat pṛcchet*), that is untenable; for in that context, the word (*śabda*) is the instrument, not the object (*artha*).

This is not a fault. It should be explained in the same way that cows and other such things serve as the instruments of questioning. The term *pātakaiḥ* (by means of sins) should be understood as a complement to both [cows, seeds, and gold]: namely, "by means of the sins associated with cows, seeds, and gold. Thus, the meaning becomes: "One should question [the witness] by pointing out the sins pertaining to cows, seeds, and gold. The interrogative statement should be recited as follows: "If you speak falsely, that sin which results from stealing or killing a cow shall be yours. In this manner, one should question a Śūdra by means of the sins about to be mentioned. As for the word *pātaka*, it should be seen as referring to designations that indicate sins, because it has been stated that the primary [sins themselves] cannot function as instruments of questioning. (8.88)
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and those for the murderer of women and children,
and for the betrayer of a friend and the ungrateful— those shall be the lot of one who speaks falsely.

Those worlds characterized by hell and the like, which are attained by those who commit such acts after killing a Brahmin, shall belong to you if you speak falsely; therefore, speak the truth—this is the exhortation. Furthermore, he who betrays a friend, or destroys Brahmins and others by seizing their wives, all their property, and so forth; and he who, forgetting a service rendered, harms that very benefactor—that ungrateful person attains whatever suffering awaits him in the hereafter. (8.89)
"O Bhadra, whatever merit you have accumulated since birth—all of that would go to a dog if you were to speak otherwise. (8.90)

The meaning is that [the merit] would go to the dog and thus become fruitless for you. Others, however, state that the mention of going to a dog is for the purpose of demonstrating a fault: just as if one were to acquire excellent goods such as gold with great difficulty and then cast them into a flow of filth, such is the nature of that meritorious deed. Furthermore, it has been stated more than once that there is no transfer of merit performed by one person to another. (8.90)
O virtuous one, you who think of yourself, "I am alone"—this sage, the witness of merit and demerit, dwells eternally within your heart. (8.91)
The sage, having become silent, was the observer—the beholder—of both merit and demerit. || 9.91 ||
But who is this sage? To demonstrate the extreme nature of the danger, he says:
"The god Yama, son of Vivasvat, who resides here in your heart—if you have no dispute with him, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the land of the Kurus. (8.92)

This Yama, who is heard of by you as the one who severs the bodies, wealth, and other possessions of all living beings and restrains them with torments—he dwells right here in your heart, not at a distance. And he punishes the offender this very moment. Do not think in your mind: "This Self of mine will overlook me. For He has no "belonging" whatsoever. If there is no dispute with Him, and if He is gracious and trustworthy, what need is there for one desiring to bathe to go to the Gaṅgā for the purification of sin, or what purpose is served by going to Kurukṣetra? Whatever fruit characterized by liberation from sin is obtained there, that is obtained right here in the non-deceptive Supreme Self. For the Self of an evildoer does not become free from apprehension, thinking, "What can He do to me? Even for an atheist, such a reflection sometimes indeed arises: "The river Gaṅgā purifies; Kurukṣetra is a sanctifying region. (8.92)
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty, and blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar. (8.93)
*Kapāla* refers to a portion of a vessel such as a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) or the like; this is easily understood. || 8.93 ||
Headlong into blind darkness shall the sinner go to hell, he who, when questioned regarding the determination of dharma, speaks falsely. (8.94)

The meaning is this: he who, when questioned about a sign, speaks what is false and untrue, is seized by that sin and evil; with his feet upward and his face downward, he reaches hell—that place of torment—in a great, dense darkness. The term "blind" is used because in other darknesses something may still be seen, but there, nothing at all can be seen. 8.94.
That man who, having entered the assembly, speaks what is inconsistent with the facts and not based on direct perception, eats fish along with their bones like a blind man. (8.95)

One speaks that which is devoid of meaning and departed from truth; for example, thorns, when eaten or consumed, do not produce such pleasure as fish do. Even when there is a mere measure of pleasure through greed for wealth, great suffering nonetheless arises—this is the simile of eating too much with thorns. 8.95.
For the gods know no other man in this world to be more excellent than that learned man whose inner self (kṣetrajña) does not feel apprehension while he speaks. 8.96.

When a witness speaks, the wise one—the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*)—does not harbor doubt as to whether he will speak the truth or a falsehood; he does not suspect him thus, but is certain that "he speaks the truth. Since his own self is free from suspicion, the gods know no other person to be more excellent, superior, or most praiseworthy than such a man.

But who is this knower? And who else could there be who entertains doubt? For it is the very same self that, by means of its own effort, becomes the knower when uttering speech; and that same self is joined with what is called doubt—in the form of "What might this be? or "How might it be?"—by way of such a mental state. In that case, a real distinction [between the knower and the doubter] is untenable. This is true; however, it was stated thus by means of an imagined distinction, just as one says, "The self kills itself by means of the self. (8.96)
Hear now, O gentle one, in due order and according to their number, how many kinsmen he slays by speaking falsely in testimony regarding each case.

This section is commenced to demonstrate that false witnesses are a specific kind of sin based upon a specific kind of falsehood regarding material things. In this regard, this verse is taught by way of an address for the purpose of inspiring respect. It is understood that what is taught in secret between two people may be taken lightly as being of little consequence; however, this matter is of extremely great importance and must be heard with full attention.

The singular form *saumya* is intended to refer specifically to Bhṛgu, even though many disciples are present. In the phrase *yasmin sākṣye*, the locative case is used with a different grammatical subject (*vyadhikaraṇa*). This is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*), meaning: "in whatever legal proceeding—distinguished by a variety of objects—there is testimony, regarding that [testimony], whatever falsehood occurs because of it. Alternatively, it follows Pāṇini 2.3.37, *yasya ca bhāvena*. Or rather, since there is a distinction of testimony due to the distinction of objects, the locative is here one of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). The word *tāvat* is derived in the sense of measure (*parimāṇa*). Since a measure might be suspected of being based on abundance, he specifies it as "by number" (*saṃkhyayā*)—referring to children, women, and the elderly. The term *anupūrvaśas* is for the sake of easy comprehension; for when something is stated in successive order, it is easily understood. And the sequence intended here is that pertaining to number, because that alone will be explained subsequently in the passage beginning with "five animals," and so forth. (8.97)
One kills five by lying about cattle, ten by lying about cows;
one kills a hundred by lying about horses, and a thousand by lying about men. (8.98)

"Lying for the sake of an animal" is a compound like *śākapārthiva* (the vegetable-king). Falsehood destroys five types of kinsmen, and consequently, their fall into hell follows. These five are: the mother, the father, the wife, the husband, and the offspring.
But how can one person experience the fruit of a sin committed by another?

We say that another’s attainment of heaven, hell, and so forth, through merit, demerit, and the like performed by someone else, occurs due to association (*saṃsarga*). What is meant is that this person is abandoned by them. Alternatively, when they are killed, whatever sin belongs to them becomes his; thus, even though he does not kill, he is said to "kill," because the resulting unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa*) is identical.

And this is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*), not an injunction regarding its performance; for if it were an injunction regarding its performance, one would incur the expiation required for violence. This constitutes the expiation for giving false testimony. The progressive increase in the number of witnesses and so forth is intended to indicate the severity of the expiation, and is not meant to be taken literally. Thus, it is stated that the expiation for each subsequent case is more grave. When there is doubt as to whose slave a particular person is, any falsehood spoken therein is called "falsehood regarding persons" (*puruṣānṛta*). (8.98)
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of gold destroys both those born and those unborn;
one destroys everything by speaking falsehood regarding land. Do not, therefore, speak falsehood regarding land. (8.99)

But how can there be a conjunction with that which belongs to another when there is no contact with those who are unborn? On account of this, it is said: "He kills both the born and the unborn. It has been stated that this is a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Regarding the statement "speaking every falsehood concerning land": do not speak an untruth connected to land. [The form *vādīḥ* is derived from the rule] *smottare laṅ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.176). This direct address, "do not speak," is also for the sake of emphasis. What, then, is this so-called "land"?
This terrestrial globe, well-known as being supported by mountains and bounded by the oceans.

Indeed, who is the owner of such a vast extent of land, or who could possibly seize it? For there is no one who is a sovereign lord of the whole earth. And thus says a verse regarding the earth: "No mortal whatsoever is entitled to give me away" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 13.7.1.15). The intention is that there is no such thing as a universal monarch. "O Viśvakarman Bhauvana, you wish to give me away!"—here we hear the king being addressed by his own name and by the title of his paternal uncle, Viśvakarman Bhauvana. "He wishes to give me away. "He will deceive me; I shall sink into the midst of the water, into the very heart of the waters. When you have formed this vain resolve, I shall submerge myself in the water. By this mention of sinking into the water, she declares the fruitlessness of the resolve to give her away; just as something cast into water is rendered useless, so too is this [act of giving]. "This promise made to Kaśyapa is false. Let this promise, this vow, this declaration—"I give her to Kaśyapa"—be in vain. For I am common to all, to be enjoyed by every person. Kings merely possess the right to enforce protection; this is the intended meaning. Therefore, since there is no possibility of either giving away or seizing such an extent of land, how can there be any dispute?

True. Just as this word *bhūmi* (land) is used here, it is likewise used for fields, villages, sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*), and so forth. And in those cases, ownership certainly exists; since giving and taking away apply only to what is perceptible, there is nothing inconsistent in this. Furthermore, its "taking away" refers to that form of seizure which applies to houses and the like, not to the mere cutting down of creepers. Consequently, one who wanders upon another's field or someone who takes a bit of earth would not be considered a thief of land. As the Mīmāṃsakas have stated: "Land cannot [be given] because it is common to all" (PMS 6.7.3).

And with reference to the word *bhūmi* as denoting a specific portion [of the earth], the Blessed One Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana has recited in the *Dānadharma* section: "The duty of giving on earth must be permitted even by other kings;
for this inexhaustible treasure of Brahman has been ordained for rulers. Thus it is said.

The Mīmāṃsakas have stated that the reason land is not to be given in the Viśvajit sacrifice is precisely because they intend the entire globe: "Land shall not [be given], because it is indistinguishable with respect to all [people]" (PMS 6.7.3). The meaning is: since land is indistinguishable with respect to all persons in its suitability for walking upon and so forth, it is impossible to make it one's own; how, then, could it be given? However, according to this view, villages, cities, and the like are what must be given in the Viśvajit.

Others, however, read: "They lead the sacrificial fee between the assembly hall and the wife's hall. Since this injunction regarding a quality (the path) is impossible on the ground itself, there must also be a gift of land and so forth in this case.

Because of the use of the singular number in the word *vadan* ("speaking"), this address—"Listen, gentle one"—(MDh 8.97) refers specifically to the witness, not to the student. From the verse beginning with "But a Śūdra [is punished] for these sins" (MDh 8.88), all instances of the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) (up to MDh 8.92) are intended as inquiries directed at the Śūdra, because they form a single syntactical unit characterized by the plurality of sins and the commonality of the verb forms and other features. From the verse beginning with "Blind he may go to the house of an enemy" (MDh 8.93), all subsequent inquiries refer to the witnesses. Due to the change in the verb form (*ākhyāta-vairūpya*), there is a break in the context; furthermore, since the sequence of meaning remains consistent in the second person, the use of the third person (*prathama-puruṣa*) in the phrase "he should go" (*gantavyo gacchet*) is intended to terminate the previous subject matter. (8.99)

They say that [the property of] women in their enjoyment and sexual intercourse, as well as [property consisting of] things born in water, all kinds of gems, and those made of stone, is like [the property of] land in the waters. (8.100)

In water, whether great—as in wells, ponds, and so forth—or small, there is no fault, just as with the earth. And regarding the enjoyment of women, which is called sexual intercourse: [the question is] "By whom has this woman been enjoyed through the act of sexual union? Regarding gems (*abja*) and jewels (*ratna*): *manayaḥ* are gems; *muktādyāḥ* refers to pearls and so forth. In the case of those made of stone, such as lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) and others, the term "gems" (*ratneṣu*) is connected [to both]. Gems are indeed of two kinds: those born of water and those made of stone. Therefore, although it would have sufficed simply to say "gems," the inclusion of the two qualifiers is for the purpose of completing the verse. Those born from water are *abjāni*; those that are modifications of stone are *aśmamayāni*. (8.100)
